questions.questionText: Consider a system employing demand paging. The system's performance is being analyzed under heavy load, and it is observed that the CPU utilization is very low while the disk utilization for the paging device is very high. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT regarding this scenario? This phenomenon is known as thrashing, and it occurs when the sum of the working sets of all active processes exceeds the total physical memory available. Increasing the degree of multiprogramming by adding more processes will likely increase CPU utilization. Replacing the local page replacement policy with a global page replacement policy will always resolve this issue. Decreasing the degree of multiprogramming is a valid strategy to bring the system back to a stable state.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system employing demand paging. The system's performance is being analyzed under heavy load, and it is observed that the CPU utilization is very low while the disk utilization for the paging device is very high. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT regarding this scenario?

  1. This phenomenon is known as thrashing, and it occurs when the sum of the working sets of all active processes exceeds the total physical memory available.
     
  2. Increasing the degree of multiprogramming by adding more processes will likely increase CPU utilization.
     
  3. Replacing the local page replacement policy with a global page replacement policy will always resolve this issue.
     
  4. Decreasing the degree of multiprogramming is a valid strategy to bring the system back to a stable state.

options.label: A
options.text: This phenomenon is known as thrashing, and it occurs when the sum of the working sets of all active processes exceeds the total physical memory available.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the degree of multiprogramming by adding more processes will likely increase CPU utilization.

options.label: C
options.text: Replacing the local page replacement policy with a global page replacement policy will always resolve this issue.

options.label: D
options.text: Decreasing the degree of multiprogramming is a valid strategy to bring the system back to a stable state.

questions.explanation: A) CORRECT: This is the classic definition of thrashing. When the system spends more time swapping pages in and out than executing instructions, CPU utilization drops because processes are constantly waiting for the disk (I/O). B) INCORRECT: In a thrashing state, adding more processes only worsens the situation. Each new process competes for the already scarce page frames, further increasing the page fault rate and decreasing CPU utilization. C) INCORRECT: Global replacement can actually exacerbate thrashing because a process can steal frames from another process that is already struggling to keep its working set in memory. Local replacement is often preferred to contain the effects of thrashing to a single process. D) CORRECT: Reducing the number of active processes (decreasing the degree of multiprogramming) frees up frames for the remaining processes, allowing them to fit their working sets into memory and reducing the page fault rate.

questions.questionText: A computer system uses $46$-bit virtual addresses and $32$-bit physical addresses with a page size of $8\mathrm{~KB}$. If the system employs a $\mathbf{3}$-level hierarchical paging scheme where each page table entry (PTE) is $4\mathrm{~bytes}$, what is the size of the page table (in bytes) for the first level if it must fit exactly within one page? $2 \mathrm{~KB}$ $4 \mathrm{~KB}$ $8 \mathrm{~KB}$ $16 \mathrm{~KB}$
questions.questionHtml:
A computer system uses $46$-bit virtual addresses and $32$-bit physical addresses with a page size of $8\mathrm{~KB}$. If the system employs a $\mathbf{3}$-level hierarchical paging scheme where each page table entry (PTE) is $4\mathrm{~bytes}$, what is the size of the page table (in bytes) for the first level if it must fit exactly within one page?

  1. $2 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  2. $4 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  3. $8 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  4. $16 \mathrm{~KB}$
questions.explanation: Page Size: $8 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{13}$ bytes. Offset: $13$ bits (from page size). Virtual Address bits for Page Tables: $46-13=33$ bits. PTE Size:  $4$ bytes $=2^2$ bytes. Entries per Page: $\frac{2^{13}}{2^2}=2^{11}$ entries. This means each level can use $\mathbf{1 1}$ bits of the virtual address. Check Levels:  $11$ bits $($Level $1) + 11$ bits $($Level $2) + 11$ bits $($Level $3)= 33$ bits. This matches our requirement. Level $\mathbf{1}$ Page Table Size: Number of entries × PTE size $=2^{11} \times 2^2=2^{13}$ bytes $=8 \mathrm{~KB}$ GO Classes answered Feb 28 GO Classes comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply akash_kumar 9 commented Feb 28 reply Follow flag if in this question asked about  Page table size  for all level 1, level 2 , level3 we need to count no of total  pages requied  ? 0 0 reply Share Dacoit commented Mar 1 reply Follow flag (1 + $2^{11}$ + $2^{22}$) * 8KB 1 1 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: \begin{aligned} &\text {To ensure a system is guaranteed to be deadlock-free, the total resources } R \text { must satisfy: }\\\\ &R \geq \sum\left(\text { Max_Need }_i-1\right)+1\\\\ & 10 \geq 4(m-1)+1 \\\\ & 10 \geq 4 m-4+1 \\\\ & 10 \geq 4 m-3 \\\\ & 13 \geq 4 m \\\\ & m \leq 3.25 \end{aligned} $\text { Since } m \text { must be an integer, the maximum value is } 3 \text {. }$ GO Classes answered Feb 28 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 2 2 votes 4(m−1)+1≤10 m<=3.25 m=3 VIPIN_CHANDRA answered Feb 28 VIPIN_CHANDRA comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.excerpt: Two processes, $A$ and $B$, share a counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ initialized to $2$. Each process executes the following code segment exactly once:wait(S); /* Critical S...
questions.questionText: Two processes, $A$ and $B$, share a counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ initialized to $2$. Each process executes the following code segment exactly once: wait(S); /* Critical Section */ signal(S); Which of the following statements is/are TRUE ? The maximum number of processes that can be in the critical section simultaneously is $2$. If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ was $0$, a deadlock would occur if both processes attempted to enter. A binary semaphore would yield the same synchronization behavior as this counting semaphore. The $\verb|wait|$ operation on a counting semaphore always decrements the value, even if it is already $0$.
questions.questionHtml:
Two processes, $A$ and $B$, share a counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ initialized to $2$. Each process executes the following code segment exactly once:

wait(S);
/* Critical Section */
signal(S);


Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. The maximum number of processes that can be in the critical section simultaneously is $2$.
     
  2. If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ was $0$, a deadlock would occur if both processes attempted to enter.
     
  3. A binary semaphore would yield the same synchronization behavior as this counting semaphore.
     
  4. The $\verb|wait|$ operation on a counting semaphore always decrements the value, even if it is already $0$.

options.label: A
options.text: The maximum number of processes that can be in the critical section simultaneously is $2$.

options.label: B
options.text: If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ was $0$, a deadlock would occur if both processes attempted to enter.

options.label: C
options.text: A binary semaphore would yield the same synchronization behavior as this counting semaphore.

options.label: D
options.text: The $\verb|wait|$ operation on a counting semaphore always decrements the value, even if it is already $0$.

questions.explanation: A) TRUE: A counting semaphore initialized to $n$ allows $n$ processes into the CS. Here, $n=2$. B) TRUE: If $\verb|S = 0|$, the first process to call $\verb|wait(S)|$ will block. If both call it, both block, leading to a deadlock. C) FALSE: A binary semaphore only allows $1$ process $(0$ or $1)$. A counting semaphore with $S=2$ allows $2$ processes. D) FALSE: If $S=0$, the $\verb|wait|$ operation typically blocks the process and puts it in a queue; it does not necessarily decrement the integer below zero in all implementations , though in some definitions it becomes negative to indicate the number of blocked processes. However, in the standard "Test and Set" logic, it stops at $0$. GO Classes answered Feb 28 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Voting & Accepting an answer helps improve the community Answer: A;B ← Previous Next → ← Previous in category Next in category → Related questions

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding Paging and Segmentation? PAGING eliminates external fragmentation but can lead to internal fragmentation. SEGMENTATION suffers from external fragmentation because segments are of variable length. THRASHING occurs when the sum of the working sets of all active processes exceeds the total physical memory available. $1$ AND $2$ ONLY $2$ AND $3$ ONLY $1$ AND $3$ ONLY $1, 2,$ AND $3$
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding Paging and Segmentation?

  1. PAGING eliminates external fragmentation but can lead to internal fragmentation.
     
  2. SEGMENTATION suffers from external fragmentation because segments are of variable length.
     
  3. THRASHING occurs when the sum of the working sets of all active processes exceeds the total physical memory available.

 

  1. $1$ AND $2$ ONLY
     
  2. $2$ AND $3$ ONLY
     
  3. $1$ AND $3$ ONLY
     
  4. $1, 2,$ AND $3$
questions.explanation: TRUE: Paging uses fixed-size blocks (pages/frames), so there are no "holes" between them (no external fragmentation). However, if a process doesn't perfectly fill its last page, memory is wasted (internal fragmentation). TRUE: Segmentation uses variable-sized segments based on logical modules. As segments are loaded and deleted, small unusable gaps form between allocated segments (external fragmentation). TRUE: Thrashing is a state of high paging activity. It occurs when the system overcommits memory such that $\sum \text{Working Sets} > \text{Total Physical RAM}$, causing the CPU to spend nearly all its time swapping pages rather than executing instructions. questions.questionText: A system uses MULTILEVEL PAGING with a $32$-bit virtual address and a page size of $\mathbf{4}$ KB. The Page Table Entry (PTE) size is $\mathbf{4}$ bytes. If the system uses a $2$-level paging scheme where the first level (outer) and second level (inner) page tables both fit exactly within one disk block, what is the size of the logical address space (in number of pages) that a single outer page table entry can cover? $2^{10}$ pages $2^{12}$ pages $2^{20}$ pages $2^{22}$ pages
questions.questionHtml:
A system uses MULTILEVEL PAGING with a $32$-bit virtual address and a page size of $\mathbf{4}$ KB. The Page Table Entry (PTE) size is $\mathbf{4}$ bytes. If the system uses a $2$-level paging scheme where the first level (outer) and second level (inner) page tables both fit exactly within one disk block, what is the size of the logical address space (in number of pages) that a single outer page table entry can cover?

  1. $2^{10}$ pages
     
  2. $2^{12}$ pages
     
  3. $2^{20}$ pages
     
  4. $2^{22}$ pages
questions.explanation: Virtual Address $=32$ bits. Page Size $=4 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{12}$ bytes. Offset $= 12$ bits. PTE Size $=4$ bytes. Entries per Page Table $=\frac{4 \mathrm{~KB}}{4 \text { bytes }}=1024=2^{10}$ entries. In a $2$-level paging scheme: The $20$ bits of the page number are split into $10$ bits for the Outer Page Table and $10 $bits for the Inner Page Table. Each entry in the Outer Page Table points to one Inner Page Table. One Inner Page Table contains $1024\left(2^{10}\right)$ entries, where each entry points to exactly one page. Therefore, one entry in the outer page table covers the address space of $2^{10}$ pages. GO Classes answered Feb 26 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider the following C code snippet executed on a standard Linux system: int main() {     if (fork() == 0) {         if (fork() == 0) {             printf("A");         } else {             printf("B");         }     } else {         printf("C");     }     return 0; } Assuming all $\verb|fork()|$ calls are successful, how many times will the character '$\mathbf{A}$' be printed, and what is the total number of processes created (including the parent)? $1$ '$\text{A}$', $3$ processes $1$ '$\text{A}$', $4$ processes $2$ '$\text{A}$', $3$ processes $2$ '$\text{A}$', $4$ processes
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C code snippet executed on a standard Linux system:

int main() {
    if (fork() == 0) {
        if (fork() == 0) {
            printf("A");
        } else {
            printf("B");
        }
    } else {
        printf("C");
    }
    return 0;
}

Assuming all $\verb|fork()|$ calls are successful, how many times will the character '$\mathbf{A}$' be printed, and what is the total number of processes created (including the parent)?

  1. $1$ '$\text{A}$', $3$ processes
     
  2. $1$ '$\text{A}$', $4$ processes
     
  3. $2$ '$\text{A}$', $3$ processes
     
  4. $2$ '$\text{A}$', $4$ processes
questions.explanation: Parent Process  $(P_0):$ Executes the first $\verb|fork()|$. It receives the PID of the child (nonzero), so it enters the $\verb|else|$ block and prints ' $\mathbf{C}$ '. First Child $(P_1):$ Created by the first $\verb|fork()|$. It receives $0$, enters the first $\verb|if|$ block, and then executes the second $\verb|fork()|$. Second Child  $(P_2):$ Created by $P_1$ during the second $\verb|fork()|$. It receives $0$, enters the inner $\verb|if|$ block, and prints '$\mathbf{A}$'. $P_1$ (returning from second fork): It receives the PID of $P_2$ (non-zero), so it enters the inner $\verb|else|$ block and prints ' $\mathbf{B}$ '. Total Processes: $P_0, P_1, P_2=3$ processes. Outputs: '$\mathbf{C}$' $($from $P_0)$, '$\mathbf{B}$' $($from $P_1)$, '$\mathbf{A}$' $($from $P_2)$. Frequency of '$\mathbf{A}$'$: 1$. questions.questionText: A file system uses INDEXED ALLOCATION with a single-level index block. The disk block size is $\mathbf{4}$ KB , and each disk block address requires $\mathbf{4}$ bytes . What is the maximum possible size of a file in this system? $2 ~\text{MB}$ $4 ~\text{MB}$ $8 ~\text{MB}$ $16 ~\text{MB}$
questions.questionHtml:
A file system uses INDEXED ALLOCATION with a single-level index block. The disk block size is $\mathbf{4}$ KB, and each disk block address requires $\mathbf{4}$ bytes. What is the maximum possible size of a file in this system?

  1. $2 ~\text{MB}$
     
  2. $4 ~\text{MB}$
     
  3. $8 ~\text{MB}$
     
  4. $16 ~\text{MB}$
questions.explanation: Disk Block Size $=4 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{12}$ bytes. Disk Block Address (Pointer) Size $=4$ bytes $=2^2$ bytes. Number of pointers per Index Block $=\frac{\text { Block Size }}{\text { Address Size }}=\frac{4096}{4}=1024$ pointers. In Single-Level Indexed Allocation, one index block contains pointers to data blocks. Total Data Blocks $=1024$. Max File Size $=$ Number of pointers × Block Size. Max File Size $=1024 \times 4 \mathrm{~KB}=4096 \mathrm{~KB}=4 \mathrm{MB}$. Correct Option: (B)

The Segment Table is as follows: \[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{Segment No.} & \text{Base Address} & \text{Limit (Size)} \\ 0 & 1200 & 800 \\ 1 & 2500 & 200 \\ 2 & 4000 & 500 \\ 3 & 1000 & 300 \end{array} \] Which of the following logical addresses will result in a SEGMENTATION FAULT ? $\langle 0,430\rangle$ $\langle 1,199\rangle$ $\langle 2,500\rangle$ $\langle 3,10\rangle$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system using pure segmentation.

The Segment Table is as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{lll}
\text{Segment No.} & \text{Base Address} & \text{Limit (Size)} \\
0 & 1200 & 800 \\
1 & 2500 & 200 \\
2 & 4000 & 500 \\
3 & 1000 & 300
\end{array}
\]

Which of the following logical addresses will result in a SEGMENTATION FAULT?

  1. $\langle 0,430\rangle$
     
  2. $\langle 1,199\rangle$
     
  3. $\langle 2,500\rangle$
     
  4. $\langle 3,10\rangle$
questions.explanation: (A) $\langle 0,430\rangle$ : Segment $0$ limit is $800.~430<800$. VALID. (B) $\langle 1,199\rangle$ : Segment $1$ limit is $200$. $199<200$. VALID. (C) $\langle 2,500)$ : Segment $2$ limit is $500 $. The valid offset range is $[0,499]$. Since $500$ is not less than $500$, it is out of bounds. SEGMENTATION FAULT. (D) $\langle 3,10\rangle$ : Segment $3$ limit is $300.~10<300$. VALID. questions.questionHtml:
A system has $n$ processes and $r$ identical resource instances. Each process requires a maximum of $m$ instances. What is the minimum number of resource instances $r$ required to ensure that the system is always deadlock-free?

  1. $n(m-1)+1$
     
  2. $n m-1$
     
  3. $n(m+1)-1$
     
  4. $m(n-1)+1$
questions.explanation: Max resources each process can hold without finishing: $(m-1)$. Total resources held by $n$ processes without any finishing: $n(m-1)$. To ensure at least one process can finish (breaking the deadlock), we need one more resource. Formula: $r=n(m-1)+1$. Correct Option: A.

questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two-process synchronization code where $\verb|flag[0]|$ and $\verb|flag[1]|$ are initialized to $\verb|false|$ and $\verb|turn|$ is initialized to $0$ or $1$ randomly$:$

Process $P_i(i=0,1 ; j=1-i)$ :

while (true) {
    flag[i] = true;
    turn = j;
    while (flag[j] && turn == j);
    // CRITICAL SECTION
    flag[i] = false;
    // REMAINDER SECTION
}


Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

  1. THE SOLUTION GUARANTEES MUTUAL EXCLUSION.
     
  2. THE SOLUTION GUARANTEES PROGRESS.
     
  3. THE SOLUTION GUARANTEES BOUNDED WAITING.
     
  4. THE SOLUTION IS PRONE TO DEADLOCK.

options.label: D
options.text: THE SOLUTION IS PRONE TO DEADLOCK.

questions.explanation: Mutual Exclusion: The $\verb|turn|$ variable acts as a tie-breaker, ensuring only one process enters the Critical Section. Progress: If no process is in the CS, a process requesting entry will not be blocked by processes in the remainder section. Bounded Waiting: A process will wait at most one $\verb|turn|$ before entering. Deadlock: It is deadlock-free because the turn variable ensures someone always moves forward. Correct Options: A, B, and C.

questions.explanation: False Statements Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks Explanation: This is false because the Banker's algorithm is used for Deadlock Avoidance , not prevention. Prevention involves negating one of the four necessary conditions (like Hold and Wait), while Avoidance dynamically checks for a safe sequence. An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource Explanation: This is false. In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), an Assignment Edge goes from Resource $\rightarrow$ Process , showing the resource is held. An edge from Process $\rightarrow$ Resource is a Request Edge . True Statements Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed Explanation: True. Forcing a process to request all resources at once (or only when it has none) breaks the "Hold and Wait" condition, effectively preventing deadlocks. questions.explanation: The Deadlock-Free Formula The standard formula for a system with $n$ processes and a single resource type where each process P has a maximum requirement m is: Step-by-Step Calculation Identify the variables: * Number of processes (n) = 5. Maximum requirement for each process (m) = 2. Calculate the "Worst-Case" allocation: A deadlock occurs if every process holds one less than its maximum requirement and no resources are left. Each process holds (2 - 1) = 1 instance. Total instances held by all 5 processes in this state = 5 *1 = 5. Find the minimum k: To break the deadlock, you need at least one more resource so that one process can finish. k = 5 + 1 = 6. Final Answer: The minimum value of k is 6 . akash_kumar 9 answered Feb 27 akash_kumar 9 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Prashant-G answered Mar 23 Prashant-G comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes . If the disk uses Linked Allocation where each block (sector) contains a $4$-byte pointer to the next block, what is the minimum number of sectors required to store the entire file?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a disk with a sector size of $512$ bytes, $2000$ tracks per surface, $50$ sectors per track, and $5$ double-sided platters. A file of size $1 \mathrm{MB}(1 \mathrm{MB}=1024 \mathrm{~KB})$ is stored in the disk.

If the disk uses Linked Allocation where each block (sector) contains a $4$-byte pointer to the next block, what is the minimum number of sectors required to store the entire file?
questions.explanation: File Size = $1 \mathrm{MB}=1024 \times 1024$ bytes = $1,048,576$ bytes. Each sector size $=512$ bytes. Pointer per sector $=4$ bytes. Effective Data per sector $=512-4=508$ bytes. Number of sectors $=\left\lceil\frac{1,048,576}{508}\right\rceil \approx 2064.12$ ANSWER $\mathbf{: 2065}$ GO Classes answered Feb 21 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. The scheduler uses Preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) . A new process $P_4$ arrives at $t=3$ with a burst time of $2$. Calculate the average waiting time for all four processes (round off to $2$ decimal places).
questions.questionHtml:
Consider three processes $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ arriving at time $t=0$ with burst times $10,5 ,$ and $8$ respectively. The scheduler uses Preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). A new process $P_4$ arrives at $t=3$ with a burst time of $2$.

Calculate the average waiting time for all four processes (round off to $2$ decimal places).
questions.explanation: At $t=0$ : Ready processes are $P_1(10), P_2(5), P_3(8)$. $P_2$ is the shortest. At $t=3: P_2$ has remained $5-3=2 . P_4$ arrives with $B T=2$. Since $P_2$ and $P_4$ have equal remaining time, $P_2$ continues (tie-breaker: same process). At $t=5: P_2$ finishes. Remaining: $P_4(2), P_3(8), P_1(10) . P_4$ runs next. At $t=7: P_4$ finishes. Remaining: $P_3(8), P_1(10)$. $P_3$ runs next. At $t=15: P_3$ finishes. $P_1$ runs last. At $t=25: P_1$ finishes. Wait Times $(W T=T A T-B T)$ : $P_1: 25-10=15$ $P_2: 5-5=0$ $P_3: 15-8=7$ $P_4:(7-3)-2=2$ Average $W T: \frac{15+0+7+2}{4}=\frac{24}{4}=6.00$ GO Classes answered Feb 21 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: Initial head position $: 50.$ Queue $: 16, 24, 43, 82, 140, 170.$ SSTF moves to the nearest request: From $50$, the closest is $\mathbf{4 3}$ $($distance $7)$. Total$: 7$. From $43$, the closest is $\mathbf{2 4}$ $($distance $19)$. Total: $7+19=26$. From $24$, the closest is $\mathbf{1 6}$ $($distance $8)$. Total: $26+8=34$. From $16$, the closest remaining is $\mathbf{8 2}$ $($distance $66)$. Total: $34+66=100$. From $82$, the closest is $\mathbf{1 4 0}$ $($distance $58)$. Total: $\mathbf{1 0 0 + 5 8 = 1 5 8}$. From $140$, the closest is $\mathbf{1 7 0}$ $($distance 30). Total: $158+30=\mathbf{1 8 8}$. questions.questionText: A system has $5$ identical resource instances shared by $N$ processes. Each process requires a maximum of $2$ resource instances to complete its execution. What is the Maximum Value of $N$ for which the system is guaranteed to be Deadlock-Free ?
questions.questionHtml: A system has $5$ identical resource instances shared by $N$ processes. Each process requires a maximum of $2$ resource instances to complete its execution. What is the Maximum Value of $N$ for which the system is guaranteed to be Deadlock-Free?
questions.explanation: For a system to be guaranteed deadlock-free, the total number of resources $(R)$ must satisfy the condition: $$ R \geq \sum\left(\operatorname{Max} \operatorname{Need}_i-1\right)+1 $$ Here, $R=5$. Each process $i$ has a Max Need of $2$ . $$ \begin{aligned} & 5 \geq \sum_{i=1}^N(2-1)+1 \\\\ & 5 \geq N(1)+1 \\\\ & 4 \geq N \end{aligned} $$ So, the maximum value of $N$ is $\mathbf{4}$. If there were $5$ processes, each could hold $1$ resource and wait for another, causing a deadlock. questions.explanation: In any paging scheme, the Page Offset is determined solely by the Page Size. Page Size $=4 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{12}$ bytes. questions.questionText: Which of the following statements regarding Semaphores and Monitors is/are CORRECT ? A binary semaphore can be used to achieve Mutual Exclusion. If a process performing a $\verb|signal()|$ operation on a counting semaphore does not find any waiting processes, the semaphore value is incremented. Monitors are high-level synchronization constructs that require the programmer to manually manage the $\verb|wait()|$ and $\verb|signal()|$ operations for mutual exclusion. A counting semaphore initialized to $5$ can allow at most $5$ processes to enter the critical section simultaneously.
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements regarding Semaphores and Monitors is/are CORRECT?

  1. A binary semaphore can be used to achieve Mutual Exclusion.
     
  2. If a process performing a $\verb|signal()|$ operation on a counting semaphore does not find any waiting processes, the semaphore value is incremented.
     
  3. Monitors are high-level synchronization constructs that require the programmer to manually manage the $\verb|wait()|$ and $\verb|signal()|$ operations for mutual exclusion.
     
  4. A counting semaphore initialized to $5$ can allow at most $5$ processes to enter the critical section simultaneously.

options.label: A
options.text: A binary semaphore can be used to achieve Mutual Exclusion.

options.label: B
options.text: If a process performing a $\verb|signal()|$ operation on a counting semaphore does not find any waiting processes, the semaphore value is incremented.

options.label: C
options.text: Monitors are high-level synchronization constructs that require the programmer to manually manage the $\verb|wait()|$ and $\verb|signal()|$ operations for mutual exclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: A counting semaphore initialized to $5$ can allow at most $5$ processes to enter the critical section simultaneously.

questions.explanation: (A) CORRECT: Binary semaphores $(0$ or $1)$ are primarily used for mutual exclusion (mutex). (B) CORRECT: In a counting semaphore, the $\verb|signal()|$ (or $\verb|V|$ ) operation increments the semaphore value. If the value becomes $\leq 0$ after incrementing, it means a process was blocked and is now woken up; if $>0$, it simply increases the available resource count. (C) INCORRECT: Monitors are high-level constructs where mutual exclusion is automatically handled by the compiler/runtime. The programmer only manages synchronization via condition variables. (D) CORRECT: A counting semaphore initialized to $N$ allows $N$ processes to pass the $\verb|wait()|$ operation before blocking.

  1. THE SYSTEM IS GUARANTEED TO BE DEADLOCK-FREE IF $N=3$.
     
  2. THE SYSTEM IS GUARANTEED TO BE DEADLOCK-FREE IF $N=4$.
     
  3. THE MAXIMUM NUMBER OF PROCESSES THE SYSTEM CAN SUPPORT WITHOUT ANY POSSIBILITY OF DEADLOCK IS $3$.
     
  4. IF $N=5$, A DEADLOCK IS CERTAIN TO OCCUR.

options.label: B
options.text: THE SYSTEM IS GUARANTEED TO BE DEADLOCK-FREE IF $N=4$.

questions.explanation: $$ \begin{gathered} n(2-1)<4 \\ n(1)<4 \\ n<4 \end{gathered} $$ This means the system is guaranteed to be deadlock-free if the number of processes $n$ is $\mathbf{3}$  or fewer. THE SYSTEM IS GUARANTEED TO BE DEADLOCK-FREE IF $N=3$ : TRUE. As calculated, $n=3$ satisfies the condition $n<4$. Even in the worst-case scenario where each of the $3$ processes holds $1$ resource $($Total $= 3)$, there is still $1$ resource left in the pool to satisfy any process's request for a second copy. THE SYSTEM IS GUARANTEED TO BE DEADLOCK-FREE IF $N=4$ : FALSE. If $n=4$ , it is possible for each process to hold $1$ resource. At this point, all 4 resources are exhausted. Each process will then wait for a second resource that will never become available. This is a deadlock state. THE MAXIMUM NUMBER OF PROCESSES THE SYSTEM CAN SUPPORT WITHOUT ANY POSSIBILITY OF DEADLOCK IS $\mathbf{3}$: TRUE. This is the direct result of our inequality $n<4$. A computer system uses $\mathbf{32}$-bit virtual addresses. The system implements a two-level hierarchical paging scheme. The page size of the Outer Page Table is exactly $\mathbf{4}$ KB, and each Page Table Entry (PTE) at all levels occupies $\mathbf{8}$ bytes. The physical page frames (base page size) used for the actual process data are $\mathbf{4}$ KB in size.

Calculate the number of bits used for the inner page table index in the virtual address.
questions.explanation: Page size $=4 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{12}$ bytes, so the Page Offset is 12 bits. Outer Page Table size $=4 \mathrm{~KB}$. Since each PTE is $8$ bytes $\left(2^3\right)$, the number of entries in the Outer Page Table $=2^{12} / 2^3=2^9$. Thus, the Outer Index is $9$ bits. Remaining bits for Inner Index $=32($Total$)-12($Offset$)-9($Outer$)= 11$ bits. GO Classes answered Feb 16 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ are given. Two binary semaphores are initialized as $(A=2)$ and $(B=0)$. A shared variable $(x)$ is initialized as $(x=0)$. Each process executes the following code: wait(A); printf("*"); x = x + 1; if (x == 2) { printf("$"); signal(B); } wait(B); signal(A); printf("#"); signal(B); Which of the following outputs is possible? $***\$\#\#\#$ $**\$*\#\#\#$ $**\$\#*\#\#$ $**\$\#\#*\#$
questions.questionHtml:
Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ are given. Two binary semaphores are initialized as $(A=2)$ and $(B=0)$. A shared variable $(x)$ is initialized as $(x=0)$.

Each process executes the following code:

wait(A);
printf("*");
x = x + 1;
if (x == 2) { 
    printf("$"); 
    signal(B);
}
wait(B);
signal(A);
printf("#");
signal(B);

Which of the following outputs is possible?

  1. $***\$\#\#\#$
     
  2. $**\$*\#\#\#$
     
  3. $**\$\#*\#\#$
     
  4. $**\$\#\#*\#$
questions.explanation: Given Processes: P1, P2, P3 Semaphores: A = 2 (counting semaphore) B = 0 Shared variable x = 0 Each process executes: wait(A); printf("*"); x = x + 1; if (x == 2) { printf("$"); signal(B); } wait(B); signal(A); printf("#"); signal(B); Important Observations A = 2 → Only two processes can enter initially . → The third process waits . Each process prints: one "*" one "#" So total output must contain: 3 stars (*) 3 hashes (#) "$" prints only once because it prints when x == 2 . B = 0 initially → All processes block at wait(B) until the process where x = 2 executes signal(B) . Step-by-Step Execution (Typical Case) Step 1 Two processes enter (say P1 and P2 ). P1: wait(A) → print * P2: wait(A) → print * Output: ** Step 2 Update x P1 → x = 1 P2 → x = 2 When x = 2 printf("$") signal(B) Output: **$ Step 3 Now B = 1 , so one process continues past wait(B) . Example order: P2 continues signal(A) print # signal(B) Output **$# Step 4 Second process passes wait(B) P1 continues signal(A) print # sig

questions.questionText: Consider a system with a $\mathbf{48}$ -bit virtual address, $\mathbf{36}$ -bit physical address, and a page size of $\mathbf{16}$ KB . The system implements an Inverted Page Table to save space. Each entry in the Inverted Page Table contains: The Process ID $(16$ bits$)$ The Virtual Page Number Control bits (Valid, Dirty, Read/Write) totaling $12$ bits The Inverted Page Table is stored in main memory. To speed up the search, a Hash Table is used. The Hash Table has the same number of entries as the Inverted Page Table, and each Hash Table entry is $\mathbf{8}$ bytes. Calculate the total size (in MB) of the Inverted Page Table (including the Hash Table metadata)?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with a $\mathbf{48}$-bit virtual address, $\mathbf{36}$-bit physical address, and a page size of $\mathbf{16}$ KB. The system implements an Inverted Page Table to save space.

Each entry in the Inverted Page Table contains:

  • The Process ID $(16$ bits$)$
     
  • The Virtual Page Number
     
  • Control bits (Valid, Dirty, Read/Write) totaling $12$ bits
     

The Inverted Page Table is stored in main memory. To speed up the search, a Hash Table is used. The Hash Table has the same number of entries as the Inverted Page Table, and each Hash Table entry is $\mathbf{8}$ bytes.

Calculate the total size (in MB) of the Inverted Page Table (including the Hash Table metadata)?
questions.explanation: NUMBER OF ENTRIES: In an Inverted Page Table, the number of entries = Number of Physical Frames. Physical Address $=36$ bits. Page Size $=16 \mathrm{~KB}\left(2^{14}\right)$. Number of Frames $=2^{36} / 2^{14}=2^{22}$ entries. SIZE OF ONE IPT ENTRY: $\mathrm{VPN}=$ Virtual Address $( 48 ) -$ Page Offset $( 14 ) = 34$ bits. Entry $=$ PID $(16) +$ VPN $(34) +$ Control $(12) = 62$ bits. Since memory is byte-addressable, we round $62$ bits up to $\mathbf{8}$ bytes per entry. TOTAL SIZE: IPT Size $=2^{22} \times 8$ bytes $=2^{22} \times 2^3=2^{25}=32 \mathrm{MB}$. Hash Table Size $=2^{22} \times 8$ bytes $=32 \mathrm{MB}$. Total $=32 \mathrm{MB}($IPT$)+32 \mathrm{MB}($Hash$)=64 \mathrm{MB}$. GO Classes answered Feb 10 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. The current allocation and request state is as follows: $P_1$ holds one instance of $R_1$ and requests one instance of $R_2$. $P_2$ holds one instance of $R_2$ and requests one instance of $R_1$. $P_3$ holds one instance of $R_1$ and one instance of $R_2$. $P_3$ now requests one instance of $R_1$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE? THE SYSTEM IS IN A DEADLOCK STATE. THERE IS A CYCLE IN THE RESOURCE ALLOCATION GRAPH. $P_3$ IS THE ONLY PROCESS PREVENTING A DEADLOCK. IF $P_3$ RELEASES ALL ITS RESOURCES, THE REMAINING PROCESSES CAN FINISH.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with $3$ processes $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and two resource types $R_1$ and $R_2$.

  • $R_1$ has $\mathbf{2}$ instances.
     
  • $R_2$ has $\mathbf{2}$ instances.

The current allocation and request state is as follows:

  • $P_1$ holds one instance of $R_1$ and requests one instance of $R_2$.
     
  • $P_2$ holds one instance of $R_2$ and requests one instance of $R_1$.
     
  • $P_3$ holds one instance of $R_1$ and one instance of $R_2$.
     
  • $P_3$ now requests one instance of $R_1$.
     

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. THE SYSTEM IS IN A DEADLOCK STATE.
     
  2. THERE IS A CYCLE IN THE RESOURCE ALLOCATION GRAPH.
     
  3. $P_3$ IS THE ONLY PROCESS PREVENTING A DEADLOCK.
     
  4. IF $P_3$ RELEASES ALL ITS RESOURCES, THE REMAINING PROCESSES CAN FINISH.

options.label: A
options.text: THE SYSTEM IS IN A DEADLOCK STATE.

options.label: B
options.text: THERE IS A CYCLE IN THE RESOURCE ALLOCATION GRAPH.

options.label: C
options.text: $P_3$ IS THE ONLY PROCESS PREVENTING A DEADLOCK.

options.label: D
options.text: IF $P_3$ RELEASES ALL ITS RESOURCES, THE REMAINING PROCESSES CAN FINISH.

questions.explanation: RESOURCES AVAILABLE: Total $(2,2)$. Currently allocated: $P_1(1,0), P_2(0,1), P_3(1,1)$. Total allocated $=(2,2)$. Available $=(0,0)$. REQUESTS: $P_1 \rightarrow R_2, P_2 \rightarrow R_1, P_3 \rightarrow R_1$. Since Available is $(0,0)$, no process can satisfy its request. CYCLE: $P_1 \rightarrow R_2 \rightarrow P_3 \rightarrow R_1 \rightarrow P_1$ (and others exist). In a multiple-instance resource graph, a cycle is a necessary but not always sufficient condition for deadlock, but here, no work can proceed. Thus, it is a deadlock. OPTION D IS FALSE: Even if $P_3$ finishes and releases $(1,1), P_1$ and $P_2$ would still be stuck in a circular wait for each other's next requirement if they both need more than what is released. questions.questionText: A system uses a $\mathbf{2-}$ level hierarchical page table for a $32-$bit virtual address space. The page size is $\mathbf{4 ~KB}$. Each Page Table Entry (PTE) at both levels is $\mathbf{4~bytes}$. The system uses a Translation Lookahead Buffer (TLB) with a hit ratio of $\mathbf{9 5 \%}$. A process is currently executing a loop where it accesses a specific data array. Due to a unique hardware constraint, the first-level page table (Page Directory) is not cacheable in the TLBonly the second-level PTEs are cached. If a TLB hit takes $\mathbf{2 ~ n s}$ and a single main memory access takes $\mathbf{100 ~ns}$, what is the Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT) in nanoseconds for a memory reference? (Assume the secondlevel page table is always in memory and ignore page faults).
questions.questionHtml:
A system uses a $\mathbf{2-}$level hierarchical page table for a $32-$bit virtual address space. The page size is $\mathbf{4 ~KB}$. Each Page Table Entry (PTE) at both levels is $\mathbf{4~bytes}$. The system uses a Translation Lookahead Buffer (TLB) with a hit ratio of $\mathbf{9 5 \%}$.

A process is currently executing a loop where it accesses a specific data array. Due to a unique hardware constraint, the first-level page table (Page Directory) is not cacheable in the TLBonly the second-level PTEs are cached.

If a TLB hit takes $\mathbf{2 ~ n s}$ and a single main memory access takes $\mathbf{100 ~ns}$, what is the Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT) in nanoseconds for a memory reference? (Assume the secondlevel page table is always in memory and ignore page faults).
questions.explanation: TLB Hit $(95\%):$ Even on a TLB hit, the hardware constraint says we only cached the $2$nd-level entry. We still have to access the Page Directory in memory. Time $=T L B_{\text {search }}+ Mem _{\text {PageDirectory }}+ Mem _{\text {ActualData }}$ Time $=2+100+100=202 \mathrm{~ns}$ TLB Miss $(5\%):$ Must access Page Directory, then Page Table, then Data. Time $=T L B_{\text {search }}+ Mem _{\text {PageDirectory }}+ Mem _{\text {PageTable }}+ Mem _{\text {ActualData }}$ Time $=2+100+100+100=302 \mathrm{~ns}$ EMAT: $(0.95 \times 202)+(0.05 \times 302)=191.9+15.1=207 \mathrm{~ns}$. questions.questionText: Consider a uniprocessor system with three processes $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ arriving at time $t=0$. Each process has a total execution time of $20$ units. The execution profile of each process is as follows: First $20 \%$ of time: I/O BURST Next $60 \%$ of time: CPU BURST Last $20 \%$ of time: I/O BURST The OS uses a Shortest Remaining CPU Time First (SRTF) scheduling algorithm. A new process is scheduled whenever the current process finishes its CPU burst or becomes blocked on I/O. Assume all I/O operations can be overlapped perfectly and the CPU never remains idle if a process is ready. What is the total time (in units) at which all processes complete their execution?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a uniprocessor system with three processes $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ arriving at time $t=0$. Each process has a total execution time of $20$ units. The execution profile of each process is as follows:

  • First $20 \%$ of time: I/O BURST
     
  • Next $60 \%$ of time: CPU BURST
     
  • Last $20 \%$ of time: I/O BURST

The OS uses a Shortest Remaining CPU Time First (SRTF) scheduling algorithm. A new process is scheduled whenever the current process finishes its CPU burst or becomes blocked on I/O. Assume all I/O operations can be overlapped perfectly and the CPU never remains idle if a process is ready.

What is the total time (in units) at which all processes complete their execution?
questions.explanation: Each process has$:$ $\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{O}$ $(4)$, $\mathrm{CPU}$ $(12)$, $\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{O}$ $(4)$. At $t=0$, all start $\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{O}$. At $t=4$, all three are ready for $\mathrm{CPU}$. Since all have the same remaining $\mathrm{CPU}$ time $(12)$, $P_1$ runs from $4-16$. $P_2$ runs from $16-28$. $P_3$ runs from $28-40$ $P_3$ finishes its final $\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{O}$ at $40+4=44$. questions.questionText: A system uses Variable Partitioning for memory management. The total physical memory is $\mathbf{1 0 0 0 ~ K B}$, out of which $\mathbf{2 0 0~ K B}$ is occupied by the Resident OS. The remaining memory is currently allocated to three processes as follows: $\mathbf{P1}: 200$ KB $($starts at address $200)$ $\mathbf{P2}: 150$ KB $($starts at address $500)$ $\mathbf{P3}: 250$ KB $($starts at address $750)$ The gaps between processes are currently empty. A new process $\mathbf{P4}$ arrives requiring $\mathbf{2 5 0}$ KB. Consider the following two scenarios: Scenario I: The system does not support compaction. Scenario II: The system supports compaction, but it takes $\mathbf{1 ~ m s}$ to move $\mathbf{1 0 ~ K B}$ of data. Which of the following statements is TRUE ? $P4$ can be accommodated in Scenario I using the Best-Fit algorithm. In Scenario II, it will take $60$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward. In Scenario II, it will take $40$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward. $P4$ cannot be accommodated even after compaction.
questions.questionHtml:
A system uses Variable Partitioning for memory management. The total physical memory is $\mathbf{1 0 0 0 ~ K B}$, out of which $\mathbf{2 0 0~ K B}$ is occupied by the Resident OS. The remaining memory is currently allocated to three processes as follows:

  • $\mathbf{P1}: 200$ KB $($starts at address $200)$
     
  • $\mathbf{P2}: 150$ KB $($starts at address $500)$
     
  • $\mathbf{P3}: 250$ KB $($starts at address $750)$

The gaps between processes are currently empty. A new process $\mathbf{P4}$ arrives requiring $\mathbf{2 5 0}$ KB.
Consider the following two scenarios:

  1. Scenario I: The system does not support compaction.
     
  2. Scenario II: The system supports compaction, but it takes $\mathbf{1 ~ m s}$ to move $\mathbf{1 0 ~ K B}$ of data.
     

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $P4$ can be accommodated in Scenario I using the Best-Fit algorithm.
     
  2. In Scenario II, it will take $60$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward.
     
  3. In Scenario II, it will take $40$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward.
     
  4. $P4$ cannot be accommodated even after compaction.

options.label: A
options.text: $P4$ can be accommodated in Scenario I using the Best-Fit algorithm.

options.label: B
options.text: In Scenario II, it will take $60$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward.

options.label: C
options.text: In Scenario II, it will take $40$ ms to create a contiguous block for $P4$ if we move $P2$ and $P3$ upward.

options.label: D
options.text: $P4$ cannot be accommodated even after compaction.

questions.explanation: OS:  $200\mathrm{~KB}(0$ to $199)$ $\mathbf{P1}: 200$ KB $(200$ to $399)$ Hole 1:  $400$ to $499 ~(100\mathrm{~KB})$ $\mathbf{P2}: 150$ KB $(500$ to $649)$ Hole 2: $650$ to $749 ~(100\mathrm{~KB})$ $\mathbf{P3}: 250$ KB $(750$ to $1000)$ Total Used: $200+200+150+250=800 \mathrm{~KB}$. Total Free: $1000-800=\mathbf{2 0 0} \mathrm{~KB}$. The largest contiguous hole is $100 \mathrm{~KB} . ~P_4$ requires $250\mathrm{~KB}$ . Therefore, $P4$  cannot be accommodated. questions.questionText: A system has $4$ processes $(P_0$ through $P_3)$ and $3$ resource types $(R_1, R_2, R_3)$. The current state is as follows: \[ \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Process} & \text{Allocation }(R_1, R_2, R_3) & \text{Max Demand }(R_1, R_2, R_3) \\ \hline P_0 & (1, 0, 1) & (4, 3, 3) \\ \hline P_1 & (1, 1, 2) & (2, 2, 2) \\ \hline P_2 & (1, 0, 3) & (1, 1, 3) \\ \hline P_3 & (2, 0, 0) & (3, 3, 1) \\ \hline \end{array} \] The Available resource vector is $(2,1,0)$. Which of the following is a valid safe sequence? $P_1, P_2, P_0, P_3$ $P_2, P_1, P_0, P_3$ $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_0$ There is no safe sequence
questions.questionHtml:
A system has $4$ processes $(P_0$ through $P_3)$ and $3$ resource types $(R_1, R_2, R_3)$. The current state is as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\text{Process} & \text{Allocation }(R_1, R_2, R_3) & \text{Max Demand }(R_1, R_2, R_3) \\
\hline
P_0 & (1, 0, 1) & (4, 3, 3) \\
\hline
P_1 & (1, 1, 2) & (2, 2, 2) \\
\hline
P_2 & (1, 0, 3) & (1, 1, 3) \\
\hline
P_3 & (2, 0, 0) & (3, 3, 1) \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
The Available resource vector is $(2,1,0)$. Which of the following is a valid safe sequence?

  1. $P_1, P_2, P_0, P_3$
     
  2. $P_2, P_1, P_0, P_3$
     
  3. $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_0$
     
  4. There is no safe sequence
questions.explanation: 1. Need Matrix $(Need = Max - Allocation)$ $P_0:(4-1,3-0,3-1)=(3,3,2)$ $P_1:(2-1,2-1,2-2)=(1,1,0)$ $P_2:(1-1,1-0,3-3)=(0,1,0)$ $P_3:(3-2,3-0,1-0)=(1,3,1)$ 2. Simulation (Initial Available:  $\mathbf{2, 1, 0}$ ) Step 1: Can $P_1$ run? Yes $(1,1,0) \leq(2,1,0)$. $P_1$ finishes, Available becomes: $(2,1,0)+(1,1,2)=(\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{2}, \mathbf{2})$. Step 2: Can $P_2$ run? Yes $(0,1,0) \leq(3,2,2)$. $P_2$ finishes, Available becomes: $(3,2,2)+(1,0,3)=(\mathbf{4 , 2 , 5})$. Step 3: Check remaining processes: $\quad P_0$ needs $(3,3,2)$. Available $(4,2,5)$. No (Insufficient $R_2$ ). $P_3$ needs $(1,3,1)$. Available $(4,2,5)$. No (Insufficient $R_2$ ). Since $P_0$ and $P_3$ cannot be satisfied even after all other processes release their resources, the system is in an unsafe state. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a disk with $200$ tracks $(0-199)$. The disk head is currently at track $50$ and was previously at track $\mathbf{40}.$ The queue of pending requests in FIFO order is:

$\mathbf{90, 150, 25, 110, 30, 180}$

The system uses the C-SCAN scheduling algorithm. What is the total distance (in tracks) moved by the disk arm to satisfy all requests?
questions.explanation: The head moves from $50$ and services all requests greater than $50$ in order: $50 \rightarrow 90 \rightarrow 110 \rightarrow 150 \rightarrow 180 \rightarrow 199$ From $199$, the head jumps immediately back to the start $($track $0)$. Distance $=199-0=\mathbf{1 9 9}$ tracks. The head moves from $0$ to service requests $25$ and $30$. $0 \rightarrow 25 \rightarrow 30$ Distance $=30-0=\mathbf{3 0}$ tracks. Total $=149($Forward$)+199($Jump$)+30($Return Service$)=\mathbf{3 7 8}$ GO Classes answered Feb 7 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Three processes ( $P_1, P_2, P_3$ ) share a single resource and coordinate using two binary semaphores, $S_1$ and $S_2$, both initialized to $0$. The processes execute the following code snippets: \[ \begin{array}{lll} P_1 & P_2 & P_3 \\ \hline \verb|print("A")| & \verb|wait(S1)| & \verb|wait(S2)| \\ \verb|signal(S1)| & \verb|print("B")| & \verb|print("C")| \\ \verb|signal(S2)| & \verb|signal(S2)| & \verb|wait(S1)| \end{array} \] Which of the following execution sequences is NOT possible? $\verb|A B C|$ $\verb|A C B|$ $\verb|B A C|$ $\verb|A|$ followed by $P_2$ and $P_3$ in any order
questions.questionHtml:
Three processes ( $P_1, P_2, P_3$ ) share a single resource and coordinate using two binary semaphores, $S_1$ and $S_2$, both initialized to $0$. The processes execute the following code snippets:

\[
\begin{array}{lll}
P_1 & P_2 & P_3 \\
\hline
\verb|print("A")| & \verb|wait(S1)| & \verb|wait(S2)| \\
\verb|signal(S1)| & \verb|print("B")| & \verb|print("C")| \\
\verb|signal(S2)| & \verb|signal(S2)| & \verb|wait(S1)|
\end{array}
\]
Which of the following execution sequences is NOT possible?

  1. $\verb|A B C|$
     
  2. $\verb|A C B|$
     
  3. $\verb|B A C|$
     
  4. $\verb|A|$ followed by $P_2$ and $P_3$ in any order

options.label: D
options.text: $\verb|A|$ followed by $P_2$ and $P_3$ in any order

questions.explanation: This is a dependency problem. We analyze the initial states of the semaphores: $S_1=0$, $S_2=0$. $P_2$ is stuck at $\verb|wait(S1)|$. It cannot print "$\verb|B|$" until $S_1>0$. $P_3$ is stuck at $\verb|wait(S2)|$. It cannot print "$\verb|C|$" until $S_2>0$. Only $P_1$ can start because it does not have an initial $\verb|wait|$. $\verb|A B C|:$ Possible. $P_1$ finishes, then $P_2$ runs, then $P_3$ runs. $\verb|A C B|:$ Possible. $P_1$ finishes, then $P_3$ runs, then $P_2$ runs. $\verb|B A C|:$ IMPOSSIBLE . "$\verb|B|$" cannot be printed before "$\verb|A|$" because $P_2$ is waiting for the signal that $P_1$ sends after printing "$\verb|A|$". $\verb|A|$ followed by  $P2$ and  $P3$: Possible. Once $P_1$ signals both, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are in the ready queue and can be interleaved. GO Classes answered Feb 7 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Consider a system with a $48$-bit virtual address and a page size of $8$ KB . The system uses a $3$-level paging scheme where the first $10$ bits index the outer page table, the next $10$ bits index the middle page table, and the remaining bits (before the offset) index the inner page table. Assume each Page Table Entry (PTE) is $8$ bytes and the TLB has $512$ entries.

If a process is currently using $20$ MB of contiguous virtual memory, what is the minimum total memory (in KB) required to store its page tables?

  1. $24$ KB
     
  2. $32$ KB
     
  3. $40$ KB
     
  4. $48$ KB
questions.explanation: Virtual Address $: 48$ bits. Page Size: $8 \mathrm{~KB}\left(2^{13}\right.$ bytes $) \rightarrow$ Offset $=13$ bits. VPN (Virtual Page Number): $48-13=35$ bits. Outer $($Level $1): 10$ bits Middle $($Level $2): 10$ bits Inner $($Level $3): 15$ bits $(35-10-10=15)$ Total Pages needed for $\mathbf{20}$ MB: $$ \frac{20 \times 1024 \mathrm{~KB}}{8 \mathrm{~KB}}=2560 \text { pages } $$ Level  $\mathbf{3}$ (Inner): One Level $3$ table entry points to one $8$ KB page. One Level $3$ table has $2^{15}$ entries. Since $2560<2^{15}$, we only need $\mathbf{1}$ Inner Page Table. Level $\mathbf{2}$ (Middle): One Level $2$ table entry points to one Level $3$ table. Since we only have $1$ Inner Table, we only need $\mathbf{1}$ Middle Page Table. Level  $\mathbf{1}$ (Outer): One Level $1$ table entry points to one Level $2$ table. We only need $\mathbf{1}$ Outer Page Table. $$ \text { Total Memory }=(1 \text { Outer }+1 \text { Middle }+1 \text { Inner }) \times 8 \mathrm{~KB}=\mathbf{2 4

Each entry in the inverted page table stores the Process ID $( 16$ bits$)$ and the Virtual Page Number. If we ignore any overhead for hashing or chaining, what is the size of the Inverted Page Table?

questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate the number of physical frames The number of physical frames is determined by the physical address space and the page size. Physical address space = 32 bits Page size = 8 KB = $2^{13}$ bytes The number of frames (entries in the IPT) is: $\text{Number of frames} = \frac{\text{Total physical memory}}{\text{Page size}} = \frac{2^{32} \text{ bytes}}{2^{13} \text{ bytes}} = 2^{(32-13)} = 2^{19}$ Step 2: Determine the size of each entry Each entry stores a Process ID (16 bits) and a Virtual Page Number (VPN). Process ID size = 16 bits = 2 bytes Virtual address space = 48 bits. Page offset is 13 bits (same as page size). So, VPN size = $48 - 13 = 35$ bits. VPN size in bytes = $\lceil 35 / 8 \rceil = 5$ bytes. Total size of one entry: $\text{Entry size} = \text{PID size} + \text{VPN size} = 2 \text{ bytes} + 5 \text{ bytes} = 7 \text{ bytes}$ Step 3: Calculate the total size of the Inverted Page Table The total size is the number of entries multiplied by the size of each entr

questions.explanation: Completion time of process P₂ Step 1: Simulate the Round Robin scheduling The processes $P_1$, $P_2$, and $P_3$ arrive at $t=0$ with burst times of 10, 20, and 30 units, respectively, and a time quantum of 10 units. The context switch overhead is 2 units. The sequence of execution is as follows: $P_1$ runs from $t=0$ to $t=10$. $P_1$ completes its burst. Context switch occurs (2 units). Time is $10+2=12$. $P_2$ runs from $t=12$ to $t=22$ (quantum). Remaining burst for $P_2$ is $20-10=10$. Context switch occurs (2 units). Time is $22+2=24$. $P_3$ runs from $t=24$ to $t=34$ (quantum). Remaining burst for $P_3$ is $30-10=20$. Context switch occurs (2 units). Time is $34+2=36$. $P_1$ is complete. $P_2$ runs from $t=36$ to $t=46$ (remaining 10 units). $P_2$ completes its burst. Step 2: Determine the completion time of $P_2$ Process $P_2$ finishes its execution at $t=46$ units. Answer:  The completion time of process $P_2$ is 46 UNITS (Option B). questions.questionHtml:
Consider a counting semaphore $S$ initialized to $10$. The following operations are performed on $S$ in the given order:

  • $\mathbf{12} ~P(S)$ operations
     
  • $\mathbf{7} ~V(S)$ operations
     
  • $\mathbf{5} ~P(S)$ operations
     
  • $\mathbf{x} ~V(S)$ operations

If the final value of the semaphore is $\mathbf{3}$, what is the value of $\mathbf{x}$ ?
questions.explanation: Initial value: $S=10$ $\mathbf{12} ~P(S)$ operations: $10-12=-2$ $\mathbf{7} ~ V(S)$ operations: $-2+7=5$ $\mathbf{5} ~ P(S)$ operations: $5-5=0$ $\mathbf{x} ~ V(S)$ operations: $0+\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{x}$ The problem states the final value is $3$. Therefore: $\mathrm{x}=3$ GO Classes answered Feb 5 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: The enter_CS() and leave_CS() functions to implement critical section of a process are realized using test-and-set instruction as follows: void enter_CS(x)  {  while (test-and-set(x)); }  void leave_CS(x) {  x = 0;  } In the above solution, x is a memory location associated with the CS and is initialized to 0. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE? Options: The above solution to CS problem is deadlock-free. The solution is starvation free. The above solution to CS problem can lead to deadlock. No more than one process can enter CS at the same time.
questions.questionHtml:
The enter_CS() and leave_CS() functions to implement critical section of a process are realized using test-and-set instruction as follows:

void enter_CS(x) 

{

 while (test-and-set(x));

} 

 

void leave_CS(x)

{

 x = 0; 

}

In the above solution, x is a memory location associated with the CS and is initialized to 0.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

Options:

  1. The above solution to CS problem is deadlock-free.

  2. The solution is starvation free.

  3. The above solution to CS problem can lead to deadlock.

  4. No more than one process can enter CS at the same time.

questions.questionText: Consider a disk with a sector size of $\mathbf{512}$ bytes , a block size of $\mathbf{2}$ KB , and a total disk capacity of $\mathbf{1 2 8 ~ G B}$. The file system uses Linked Allocation to manage files. If a specific file has a size of $\mathbf{1 8 ~ K B}$, how many bytes of the disk's total capacity are used solely for pointers to manage this file? (Assume each pointer requires $\mathbf{4}$  bytes and is stored within the data block). Note: The pointer to the first block of the file is stored in the directory entry and should NOT be counted.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a disk with a sector size of $\mathbf{512}$ bytes, a block size of $\mathbf{2}$ KB , and a total disk capacity of $\mathbf{1 2 8 ~ G B}$. The file system uses Linked Allocation to manage files. If a specific file has a size of $\mathbf{1 8 ~ K B}$, how many bytes of the disk's total capacity are used solely for pointers to manage this file? (Assume each pointer requires $\mathbf{4}$ bytes and is stored within the data block).

Note: The pointer to the first block of the file is stored in the directory entry and should NOT be counted.
questions.explanation: <!--td {border: 1px solid #cccccc;}br {mso-data-placement:same-cell;}--> Sector size is $512$ bytes. Block size is $2$ KB $= 2048$ bytes. Total disk capacity is $128$ GB (not directly needed for this calculation). File size is $18$ KB $= 18432$ bytes. Allocation method is Linked Allocation. Pointer size is $4$ bytes and stored inside each data block. Number of Blocks Used by the File: Blocks required $=18432 \div 2048=9$ blocks (The file fits exactly, so no partial block.) Pointer Overhead in Linked Allocation: In linked allocation, each data block contains one pointer to the next block. So, number of pointers $=$ number of blocks $=9$. Total Bytes Used Only for Pointers: Pointer space $=9 \times 4$ bytes $=36$ bytes. GO Classes answered Feb 3 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Two processes, $P_0$ and $P_1$, share a counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ initialized to $2$ and a binary semaphore $\verb|mutex|$ initialized to $1$. They execute the following code concurrently: Process $P_0$ : wait(S); wait(mutex); // Critical Section signal(mutex); signal(S); Process $P_1$ : wait(S); wait(mutex); // Critical Section signal(nutex); signal(S): Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding the execution of these processes? Mutual exclusion is preserved for the Critical Section. Deadlock is possible if both processes execute $\verb|wait(S)|$ simultaneously. At most two processes can be in the Critical Section at any given time. If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ is changed to $1$, the behavior of the system remains functionally identical to using only the $\verb|mutex|$.
questions.questionHtml:
Two processes, $P_0$ and $P_1$, share a counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ initialized to $2$ and a binary semaphore $\verb|mutex|$ initialized to $1$. They execute the following code concurrently:

Process $P_0$ :

wait(S);
wait(mutex);
// Critical Section
signal(mutex);
signal(S);


Process $P_1$ :

wait(S);
wait(mutex);
// Critical Section
signal(nutex);
signal(S):


Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding the execution of these processes?

  1. Mutual exclusion is preserved for the Critical Section.
     
  2. Deadlock is possible if both processes execute $\verb|wait(S)|$ simultaneously.
     
  3. At most two processes can be in the Critical Section at any given time.
     
  4. If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ is changed to $1$, the behavior of the system remains functionally identical to using only the $\verb|mutex|$.

options.label: A
options.text: Mutual exclusion is preserved for the Critical Section.

options.label: B
options.text: Deadlock is possible if both processes execute $\verb|wait(S)|$ simultaneously.

options.label: C
options.text: At most two processes can be in the Critical Section at any given time.

options.label: D
options.text: If the initial value of $\verb|S|$ is changed to $1$, the behavior of the system remains functionally identical to using only the $\verb|mutex|$.

questions.explanation: A is TRUE: The $\verb|mutex|$ semaphore (binary) ensures only one process enters the Critical Section at a time, regardless of the value of $\verb|S|$. B is FALSE: Since $\verb|S|$ starts at 2 , both processes can successfully complete $\verb|wait(S)|$ without blocking. C is FALSE: Because of the $\verb|mutex|$, only one process can be in the Critical Section, not two. D is TRUE: If $\verb|S|$ is 1, it acts as another binary semaphore, and the mutex already restricts entry to one process. questions.questionText: Consider a computer system using a $3$-level paging scheme. The Virtual Address is $46$ bits, and the Physical Address is $32$ bits. The page size is $\mathbf{8 ~ K B}$. The page table base register (PTBR) stores the base address of the first-level table $(T_1)$, which occupies exactly one page. Each entry in $T_1$ points to a second-level table $\left(T_2\right)$, and each entry in $T_2$ points to a third-level table ( $T_3$ ). Each entry in $T_3$ is a Page Table Entry (PTE). If the size of each PTE is $\mathbf{3 2}$ bits , what is the maximum number of entries possible in a single $T_3$ table?
questions.questionHtml: Consider a computer system using a $3$-level paging scheme. The Virtual Address is $46$ bits, and the Physical Address is $32$ bits. The page size is $\mathbf{8 ~ K B}$. The page table base register (PTBR) stores the base address of the first-level table $(T_1)$, which occupies exactly one page. Each entry in $T_1$ points to a second-level table $\left(T_2\right)$, and each entry in $T_2$ points to a third-level table ( $T_3$ ). Each entry in $T_3$ is a Page Table Entry (PTE). If the size of each PTE is $\mathbf{3 2}$ bits, what is the maximum number of entries possible in a single $T_3$ table?
questions.explanation: The page size is $8 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{13}$ bytes. Since the first-level table $T_1$ occupies exactly one page and each PTE (or pointer to the next level) is $32$ bits $( 4$ bytes$)$, the number of entries per page is: $$ \frac{2^{13}}{2^2}=2^{11}=2048 \text { entries } $$ This structure remains consistent for each level if they are all page-sized. Therefore, a single $T_3$ table can hold $2048$ entries. Consider the linear page table for this process. Only \(4\) valid PTEs are explicitly marked; all remaining PTEs are invalid. $$ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{PTE index} & \text{PTE status} \\ \hline 0 & \text{valid} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \hline 10 & \text{valid} \\ \hline \vdots & \vdots \\ 14 & \text{valid} \\ 15 & \text{valid} \end{array} $$ To implement a multi-level page table, the linear page table is divided into page-sized chunks. A chunk is allocated only if it contains at least one valid PTE. How many entries in the outermost page table (page directory) are valid?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a process with a $64$-byte virtual address space and a page size of \(4\) bytes. Each page table entry (PTE) occupies $1$ byte.

Consider the linear page table for this process. Only \(4\) valid PTEs are explicitly marked; all remaining PTEs are invalid.

$$ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{PTE index} & \text{PTE status} \\ \hline 0 & \text{valid} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \hline 10 & \text{valid} \\ \hline \vdots & \vdots \\ 14 & \text{valid} \\ 15 & \text{valid} \end{array} $$

To implement a multi-level page table, the linear page table is divided into page-sized chunks. A chunk is allocated only if it contains at least one valid PTE.

How many entries in the outermost page table (page directory) are valid?
questions.explanation: Virtual address space = \(64\) bytes and page size = \(4\) bytes. \[ \Rightarrow \text{Number of virtual pages} = \frac{64}{4} = 16 \] Each page table entry occupies \(1\) byte. Hence, the linear page table contains \(16\) entries and has a total size of \(16\) bytes. The linear page table is divided into page-sized chunks of \(4\) bytes. \[ \Rightarrow \text{Number of chunks} = \frac{16}{4} = 4 \] Each chunk corresponds to one entry in the outermost page table (page directory). From the given linear page table: PTEs \(0\)–\(3\): contain a valid PTE PTEs \(4\)–\(7\): contain no valid PTE PTEs \(8\)–\(11\): contain a valid PTE PTEs \(12\)–\(15\): contain valid PTEs Therefore, the number of valid entries in the outermost page table is \[ \boxed{3} \] GO Classes answered Feb 1 • edited Feb 1 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Aminul_Islam 1 commented Feb 1 i edited by Aminul_Islam 1 Feb 1 reply Follow flag Total PTEs = 16 They are indexed:

questions.questionHtml:
Some arrangements of threads and the locks they attempt to acquire can lead to deadlock. Assume that once a thread acquires a lock, it holds it until all required locks are acquired.

Which of the following arrangements will NOT lead to deadlock?

  1. Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in an arbitrary order.
    Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.
  2. Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.
    Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 2$ then $1$.
  3. Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.
    Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1, 2,$ and $3$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$ then $3$.
  4. Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 2$ then $1$.
    Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 2$ then $1$.

options.label: A
options.text: Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in an arbitrary order. Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.

options.label: B
options.text: Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$. Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 2$ then $1$.

options.label: C
options.text: Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$. Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1, 2,$ and $3$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$ then $3$.

options.label: D

questions.questionText: Consider a system with three processes $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and three resource types $R_1, R_2, R_3$. Each resource type has one instance . The current allocation state is as follows: $P_1$ is holding $R_1$ and requesting $R_2$. $P_2$ is holding $R_2$ and requesting $R_3$. $P_3$ is holding $R_3$. A new request arrives: $P_3$ requests $R_1$. Which of the following statements is TRUE ? The system is in a safe state, and no deadlock occurs.  The system is in a deadlock state involving $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$.  Only $P_1$ and $P_2$ are in a deadlock.  The system is in an unsafe state, but deadlock can be avoided if $P_3$ releases $R_3$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with three processes $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and three resource types $R_1, R_2, R_3$. Each resource type has one instance. The current allocation state is as follows:

  • $P_1$ is holding $R_1$ and requesting $R_2$.
     
  • $P_2$ is holding $R_2$ and requesting $R_3$.
     
  • $P_3$ is holding $R_3$.

A new request arrives: $P_3$ requests $R_1$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. The system is in a safe state, and no deadlock occurs. 
     
  2. The system is in a deadlock state involving $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$. 
     
  3. Only $P_1$ and $P_2$ are in a deadlock. 
     
  4. The system is in an unsafe state, but deadlock can be avoided if $P_3$ releases $R_3$.

options.label: A
options.text: The system is in a safe state, and no deadlock occurs.

options.label: B
options.text: The system is in a deadlock state involving $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$.

options.label: C
options.text: Only $P_1$ and $P_2$ are in a deadlock.

options.label: D
options.text: The system is in an unsafe state, but deadlock can be avoided if $P_3$ releases $R_3$.

questions.explanation: In a Resource Allocation Graph, if every resource type has only one instance , a cycle is both a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock. $P_1$ is waiting for $R_2$, which is held by $P_2$. $P_2$ is waiting for $R_3$, which is held by $P_3$. $P_3$ is now waiting for $R_1$, which is held by $P_1$. This creates the following directed cycle: $$ P_1 \rightarrow R_2 \rightarrow P_2 \rightarrow R_3 \rightarrow P_3 \rightarrow R_1 \rightarrow P_1 $$ Conclusion: Every process in the cycle is waiting for a resource held by another process in the cycle. Since there are no other instances available to break the chain, the system is in a deadlock state involving all three processes. questions.questionText: Consider the Producer-Consumer problem with a shared buffer of size $N=5$. The system uses three semaphores$: \verb|empty|$ $($initialized to $5 )$, $\verb|full|$ $($initialized to $0 )$, and $\verb|mutex|$ $($initialized to $1)$. The Producer process executes the following code: while(true) {     // Produce item     Wait(empty);     Wait(mutex);     // Add to buffer     Signal(mutex);     Signal(full); } The Consumer process executes the following code: while(true) {     Wait(full);     Wait(mutex);     // Remove from buffer     Signal(mutex);     Signal(empty);     // Consume item } Suppose the Producer has already added $\mathbf{3}$ items to the buffer. If $\mathbf{2}$ Consumer instances and $\mathbf{1}$  Producer instance now attempt to access the buffer simultaneously, what is the maximum possible value the semaphore $\verb|empty|$ can reach during their execution?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the Producer-Consumer problem with a shared buffer of size $N=5$. The system uses three semaphores$: \verb|empty|$ $($initialized to $5 )$, $\verb|full|$ $($initialized to $0 )$, and $\verb|mutex|$ $($initialized to $1)$.

The Producer process executes the following code:

while(true) {
    // Produce item
    Wait(empty);
    Wait(mutex);
    // Add to buffer
    Signal(mutex);
    Signal(full);
}

The Consumer process executes the following code:

while(true) {
    Wait(full);
    Wait(mutex);
    // Remove from buffer
    Signal(mutex);
    Signal(empty);
    // Consume item
}

Suppose the Producer has already added $\mathbf{3}$ items to the buffer. If $\mathbf{2}$ Consumer instances and $\mathbf{1}$ Producer instance now attempt to access the buffer simultaneously, what is the maximum possible value the semaphore $\verb|empty|$ can reach during their execution?
questions.explanation: Buffer size $N=5$. $3$ items are already in the buffer. $\verb|full|$ $=3$ (counts items present). $\verb|empty| = 2$ (counts available slots: $5-3=2$). $\verb|mutex| =1$. Execution for Maximum  $\verb|empty|$  Value: To maximize $\verb|empty|$, we need the Consumers to finish their work before the Producer starts theirs. Consumer increments empty so it will become $4$ after $2$ consumers. Producer decrements empty so it will become $3$ after $1$ producer. Max possible empty during execution $= 4$ GO Classes answered Jan 30 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Each process executes the following sequence of operations exactly once: Wait(S); // Critical Section Signal(S); Wait(S); // Critical Section Signal(S); If no other processes or operations interfere with $S$, what is the maximum possible value the semaphore $S$ can reach at any point during the execution of these three processes?
questions.questionHtml:
Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ share a common counting semaphore $S$ , which is initialized to $2$. Each process executes the following sequence of operations exactly once:

Wait(S);
// Critical Section
Signal(S);
Wait(S);
// Critical Section
Signal(S);

If no other processes or operations interfere with $S$, what is the maximum possible value the semaphore $S$ can reach at any point during the execution of these three processes?
questions.explanation: The first $\verb|Wait|$ operations will always bring $S$ down. The $\verb|Signal|$ operations only happen after a process has already "consumed" a unit of the semaphore. questions.questionText: Consider a system with two priority queues for CPU scheduling: Queue $\mathbf{1}$ (High Priority) uses Round Robin (RR) with a time quantum of $\mathbf{2 ~ms}$, and Queue $\mathbf{2}$ (Low Priority) uses First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS). A process from Queue $2$ can only run if Queue $1$ is empty. If a process arrives in Queue $1$ while a process from Queue $2$ is running, the Queue $2$ process is preempted immediately. The context switching overhead is $\mathbf{0 . 5 ~ m s}$ whenever the CPU switches from one process to another (including switching between processes in the same queue). Two processes, $P_1$ and $P_2$, arrive in Queue $1$ at time $t=0$ and $t=1$ respectively, with burst times of $\mathbf{4} \mathbf{~ m s}$ each. One process $P_3$ arrives in Queue $2$ at $t=0$ with a burst time of $\mathbf{2} \mathbf{~ m s}$. What is the completion time of process $P_3$ ? $11.5 ~\mathrm{ms}$ $12.0 ~\mathrm{ms}$ $13.5 ~\mathrm{ms}$ $14.0 ~\mathrm{ms}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with two priority queues for CPU scheduling: Queue $\mathbf{1}$ (High Priority) uses Round Robin (RR) with a time quantum of $\mathbf{2 ~ms}$, and Queue $\mathbf{2}$ (Low Priority) uses First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS).

  • A process from Queue $2$ can only run if Queue $1$ is empty.
     
  • If a process arrives in Queue $1$ while a process from Queue $2$ is running, the Queue $2$ process is preempted immediately.
     
  • The context switching overhead is $\mathbf{0 . 5 ~ m s}$ whenever the CPU switches from one process to another (including switching between processes in the same queue).

Two processes, $P_1$ and $P_2$, arrive in Queue $1$ at time $t=0$ and $t=1$ respectively, with burst times of $\mathbf{4} \mathbf{~ m s}$ each. One process $P_3$ arrives in Queue $2$ at $t=0$ with a burst time of $\mathbf{2} \mathbf{~ m s}$. What is the completion time of process $P_3$ ?

  1. $11.5 ~\mathrm{ms}$
     
  2. $12.0 ~\mathrm{ms}$
     
  3. $13.5 ~\mathrm{ms}$
     
  4. $14.0 ~\mathrm{ms}$
questions.explanation: $t=0$ to $t=2: P_1$ runs for its first quantum (RR, $q=2$). Remainder: $P_1=2 \mathrm{~ms}$. $t=2$ to $t=2.5$ : Context switch from $P_1$ to $P_2$ (Overhead $=0.5 \mathrm{~ms}$). $t=2.5$ to $t=4.5: P_2$ runs for its first quantum. Remainder: $P_2=2 \mathrm{~ms}$. $t=4.5$ to $t=5.0$ : Context switch from $P_2$ back to $P_1$ (Overhead $=0.5 \mathrm{~ms}$). $t=5.0$ to $t=7.0: P_1$ runs for its final $2 \mathrm{~ms}$ and completes. $t=7.0$ to $t=7.5$ : Context switch from $P_1$ to $P_2$ (Overhead $=0.5 \mathrm{~ms}$). $t=7.5$ to $t=9.5: P_2$ runs for its final $2 \mathrm{~ms}$ and completes. $t=9.5$ to $t=10.0$ : Queue $1$ is now empty. Context switch from $P_2$ to $P_3$ (Overhead $= 0.5 \mathrm{~ms}$). $t=10.0$ to $t=12.0: P_3$ runs for its $2 \mathrm{~ms}$ burst and completes. The processes execute the following code: Process $P_1$ : wait(S); count = count + 5; signal(S); Process $P_2$ : wait(S); count = count * 2; signal(S); If these processes are executed concurrently, what is the difference between the maximum possible value and the minimum possible value of count after both processes complete?

Consider two processes, $P_1$ and $P_2$, sharing a common variable count (initialized to 10) and using a binary semaphore S (initialized to 1). The processes execute the following code:

Process $P_1$ :

wait(S);
count = count + 5;
signal(S);

If these processes are executed concurrently, what is the difference between the maximum possible value and the minimum possible value of count after both processes complete?
questions.explanation: Since a BINARY SEMAPHORE is used, the processes cannot interleave their internal steps; one must finish its entire operation before the other starts. We need to find the difference between the possible final values. Case $1\left(P_1\right.$ then $\left.P_2\right)$ : 1. Start with 10. 2. $P_1$ adds 5: $10+5=15$. 3. $P_2$ multiplies by 2 : $15 \times 2=\mathbf{3 0}$. Case $2\left(P_2\right.$ then $\left.P_1\right)$ : 1. Start with 10. 2. $P_2$ multiplies by 2 : $10 \times 2=20$. 3. $P_1$ adds $5: 20+5=\mathbf{2 5}$. Difference = 5 GO Classes answered Jan 28 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Which of the following is/are correct?

  2. THE NUMBER OF ENTRIES IN THE OUTER PAGE TABLE IS 1024.
     
  3. THE TOTAL NUMBER OF BITS USED FOR PAGING INDEXES (OUTER + INNER) IS 22 BITS.

options.label: A
options.text: THE INNER PAGE TABLE REQUIRES 10 BITS FOR INDEXING.

options.label: B
options.text: THE NUMBER OF ENTRIES IN THE OUTER PAGE TABLE IS 1024.

options.label: C

questions.explanation: ENTRIES PER PAGE: Since a page is 4 KB and each entry is 4 bytes, one page frame can hold $\frac{4096}{4}=1024$ entries $\left(2^{10}\right)$. No of pages $=\mathbf{2^{\boldsymbol{ 20}}}$ No of inner pages required = $2^{20} / 1024 = 1024$ No of entries in outer page table = 1024 (D) Each inner page table also uses 10 bits ( $2^{10}$ entries), so it also fits in one frame. questions.questionText: Consider a system with three processes $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ that arrive at time $t=0$ in that order. The total CPU burst time for each process is $10$ units. However, each process follows a specific execution pattern: it executes on the CPU for $2$ units, then performs an I/O operation for $5$ units, and finally returns for its remaining $8$ units of CPU burst. If the system uses Preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling and I/O operations can happen in parallel, what is the finish time of the last process to complete?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with three processes $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ that arrive at time $t=0$ in that order. The total CPU burst time for each process is $10$ units. However, each process follows a specific execution pattern: it executes on the CPU for $2$ units, then performs an I/O operation for $5$ units, and finally returns for its remaining $8$ units of CPU burst.

If the system uses Preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling and I/O operations can happen in parallel, what is the finish time of the last process to complete?
questions.explanation: Total CPU burst for each: 2 (initial) +8 (final) = 10 units. 1. $t=0$ to $t=2$ : $P_1$ runs (SRTF tie-break). At $t=2, P_1$ finishes its first burst and goes to I/O for 5 units (ready at $t=7$ ). 2. $t=2$ to $t=4: P_2$ runs. At $t=4, P_2$ goes to $\mathrm{I} / \mathrm{O}$ for 5 units (ready at $t=9$ ). 3. $t=4$ to $t=6: P_3$ runs. At $t=6, P_3$ goes to I/O for 5 units (ready at $t=11$ ). 4. $t=6$ to $t=7$ : CPU is IDLE (All processes are in I/O). 5. $t=7$ to $t=15: P_1$ returns from I/O. Its remaining burst is 8 . It finishes at $t=15$. 6. $t=15$ to $t=23: P_2$ returns (at $t=9$ ) and runs its 8 units. It finishes at $t=23$. 7. $t=23$ to $t=31: P_3$ returns (at $t=11$ ) and runs its 8 units. It finishes at $t=31$. GO Classes answered Jan 28 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment.   3. THE PAGE TABLE SIZE EXCEEDS THE AVAILABLE CACHE (TLB) SPACE.
     
  4. THE DISK SCHEDULING ALGORITHM IS INEFFICIENCT (E.G., FCFS INSTEAD OF SSTF).

questions.explanation: THE SUM OF THE WORKING SET SIZES OF ALL ACTIVE PROCESSES EXCEEDS THE TOTAL PHYSICAL MEMORY. When the system cannot fit the active working sets in RAM, it enters a constant cycle of page faults and swapping, leading to thrashing. THE DISK SCHEDULING ALGORITHM IS INEFFICIENCT (E.G., FCFS INSTEAD OF SSTF). While inefficient, this affects latency and throughput but is not the root cause of process-level thrashing. Correct option: B

The following table shows the current allocation and maximum requirements for four processes $(P 0$ through $P 3):$ \[ \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{Process} & \textbf{Allocation (R1, R2, R3)} & \textbf{Max Demand (R1, R2, R3)} \\ \hline P0 & (0,1,0) & (7,5,3) \\ \hline P1 & (2,0,0) & (3,2,2) \\ \hline P2 & (3,0,2) & (9,0,2) \\ \hline P3 & (2,1,1) & (2,2,2) \\ \hline \end{array} \] Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
