questions.questionText: Consider the following C program executed on a UNIX-like system: #include <stdio.h> #include <unistd.h> int main() {     int x = 1;         if (fork() && fork()) {         x = x + 2;     } else {         x = x + 1;     }         printf("%d\n", x);     return 0; } Which of the following statements is/are correct? Exactly $3$ processes are created in total Exactly $4$ processes are created in total The value $\verb|3|$ is printed exactly once The value $\verb|2|$ is printed more than once
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C program executed on a UNIX-like system:
 

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    int x = 1;
    
    if (fork() && fork()) {
        x = x + 2;
    } else {
        x = x + 1;
    }
    
    printf("%d\n", x);
    return 0;
}


Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. Exactly $3$ processes are created in total
     
  2. Exactly $4$ processes are created in total
     
  3. The value $\verb|3|$ is printed exactly once
     
  4. The value $\verb|2|$ is printed more than once

options.label: A
options.text: Exactly $3$ processes are created in total

options.label: B
options.text: Exactly $4$ processes are created in total

options.label: C
options.text: The value $\verb|3|$ is printed exactly once

options.label: D
options.text: The value $\verb|2|$ is printed more than once

questions.explanation: Initial process $\text{P0}$ starts with $\mathrm{x}=1$. Expression is $\verb|fork() && fork()|$ with short-circuit AND. In $\text{P0}$, first $\verb|fork()|$ is executed. $\text{P0}$ gets non-zero → evaluates second $\verb|fork()|$ . Child $\text{C1}$ gets $0 \rightarrow$ short-circuit applies, second fork() is NOT executed in $\text{C1}$. Now from $\text{P0}$'s second $\verb|fork()|$ : Parent $\text{P0}$ gets non-zero. Child $\text{C2}$ gets $0$. Total processes: $\mathrm{P0}, \mathrm{C} 1, \mathrm{C} 2 \rightarrow 3$ processes. So option A is correct, option B is false. Which Branch Executes: $\text{P0}:$first fork true AND second fork true → condition true $\rightarrow x=1+2=3$ $\text{C1}:$ first fork false → goes to else $\rightarrow x=1+1=2$ $\text{C2}:$ first fork true, second fork false → condition false → else → $\mathrm{x}=1+1=2$ Output Analysis: Value $3$ is printed once (by $\text{P0}$). questions.questionText: A counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ is initialized to $3.$ Five identical processes $\text{P1}-\text{P5}$ execute the following code concurrently: wait(S); /* critical section */ signal(S); Assume no process terminates inside the critical section. Which of the following statements is/are correct? At most $3$ processes can be in the critical section at any time Deadlock is possible Starvation is possible if semaphore scheduling is unfair Exactly $3$ processes will always be in the critical section
questions.questionHtml:
A counting semaphore $\verb|S|$ is initialized to $3.$

Five identical processes $\text{P1}-\text{P5}$ execute the following code concurrently:

wait(S);
/* critical section */
signal(S);

Assume no process terminates inside the critical section.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. At most $3$ processes can be in the critical section at any time
     
  2. Deadlock is possible
     
  3. Starvation is possible if semaphore scheduling is unfair
     
  4. Exactly $3$ processes will always be in the critical section

options.label: A
options.text: At most $3$ processes can be in the critical section at any time

options.label: C
options.text: Starvation is possible if semaphore scheduling is unfair

options.label: D
options.text: Exactly $3$ processes will always be in the critical section

questions.explanation: The semaphore $\verb|S|$ is initialized to $3$ , so at most $3 ~\verb|wait(S)|$ operations can succeed simultaneously. Hence, at most $3$ processes can be in the critical section at any time. Option A is correct. Deadlock is not possible because every process that enters the critical section eventually executes $\verb|signal(S)|$, and there is no circular wait. Option B is false. Starvation is possible if the semaphore implementation uses unfair scheduling. A process may remain waiting indefinitely while others repeatedly enter the critical section. Option C is correct. It is not guaranteed that exactly 3 processes will always be in the critical section, since fewer than $3$ may be executing or ready at some times. Option D is false. Correct options: A, C

questions.questionText: Two processes $\text{P1}$ and $\text{P2}$ share two semaphores $\verb|S|$ and $\verb|T|$, both initialized to $1$. The code executed by the processes is: $\textbf{P1} : $ wait(S); wait(T); /* critical section */ signal(T); signal(S); $\textbf{P2} : $ wait(T); wait(S); /* critical section */ signal(S); signal(T); Which of the following statements is/are correct? Mutual exclusion is guaranteed Deadlock is possible Starvation is possible Both processes can be in the critical section at the same time
questions.questionHtml:
Two processes $\text{P1}$ and $\text{P2}$ share two semaphores $\verb|S|$ and $\verb|T|$, both initialized to $1$.

The code executed by the processes is:

$\textbf{P1} : $

wait(S);
wait(T);
/* critical section */
signal(T);
signal(S);


$\textbf{P2} : $

wait(T);
wait(S);
/* critical section */
signal(S);
signal(T);


Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. Mutual exclusion is guaranteed
     
  2. Deadlock is possible
     
  3. Starvation is possible
     
  4. Both processes can be in the critical section at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: Both processes can be in the critical section at the same time

questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion is guaranteed because both processes must successfully execute $\verb|wait(S)|$ and $\verb|wait(T)|$ before entering the critical section. Since $\verb|S|$ and $\verb|T|$ are binary semaphores, only one process can hold each at a time. So option A is correct. Deadlock is possible because $\text{P1}$ may acquire $\verb|S|$ and wait for $\verb|T|$, while simultaneously $\text{P2}$ acquires $\verb|T|$ and waits for $\verb|S|$. This circular wait leads to deadlock. So option B is correct. Starvation is not inherent in this code. If deadlock does not occur, each process eventually releases the semaphores. Starvation is not guaranteed by the structure itself. So option C is false. Both processes cannot be in the critical section at the same time because they must acquire both semaphores before entering. So option D is false. Correct options: A, B

questions.questionText: A demand-paged system has the following characteristics: Memory access time $\mathrm{= 200 ~ns}$ Page fault service time $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$ Probability of a page fault $\mathrm{= p}$ The effective memory access time (EMAT) must not exceed $\mathrm{300 ~ns}$ Which of the following is the maximum acceptable value of $\mathbf{p}$ ? $1 \times 10^{-6}$ $5 \times 10^{-6}$ $1 \times 10^{-5}$ $5 \times 10^{-5}$
questions.questionHtml:
A demand-paged system has the following characteristics:

  • Memory access time $\mathrm{= 200 ~ns}$
     
  • Page fault service time $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$
     
  • Probability of a page fault $\mathrm{= p}$

The effective memory access time (EMAT) must not exceed $\mathrm{300 ~ns}$

Which of the following is the maximum acceptable value of $\mathbf{p}$ ?

  1. $1 \times 10^{-6}$
     
  2. $5 \times 10^{-6}$
     
  3. $1 \times 10^{-5}$
     
  4. $5 \times 10^{-5}$
questions.explanation: Memory access time $=200 \mathrm{~ns}$ Page fault service time $=10 \mathrm{~ms}=10^7 \mathrm{~ns}$ Effective Memory Access Time formula: $$ \text { EMAT }=(1-p) \times 200+p \times\left(10^7+200\right) $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \text{EMAT} \leq 300 \mathrm{~ns}\\\\ & 200+p \times 10^7 \leq 300 \\\\ & p \times 10^7 \leq 100 \\\\ & p \leq 100 / 10^7 \\\\ & p \leq 1 \times 10^{-5} \end{aligned} $$ Correct option: C

Which of the following statements is/are correct? The number of bits required for the page offset is $10$ The number of entries in the page table is $64$ The total size of the page table is $128 ~\text{bytes}$ The number of frames in physical memory is $32$
questions.questionHtml:
A system uses paging with the following parameters:

  • Logical address space size $=64 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  • Page size $=1 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  • Physical memory size $=32 \mathrm{~KB}$
     
  • Page table entry size $=2 ~\text{bytes}$
     

Each logical address is of the form (page number, page offset).
 

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. The number of bits required for the page offset is $10$
     
  2. The number of entries in the page table is $64$
     
  3. The total size of the page table is $128 ~\text{bytes}$
     
  4. The number of frames in physical memory is $32$

options.label: A
options.text: The number of bits required for the page offset is $10$

options.label: B
options.text: The number of entries in the page table is $64$

options.label: C
options.text: The total size of the page table is $128 ~\text{bytes}$

options.label: D
options.text: The number of frames in physical memory is $32$

questions.explanation: Logical address space size $=64 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{16}$ bytes Page size $=1 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{10}$ bytes Page offset bits $=\log _2(1 \mathrm{~KB})=10$ bits So statement A is correct. Number of pages $=64 \mathrm{~KB} / 1 \mathrm{~KB}=64$ So page table has $64$ entries Statement B is correct. Page table entry size $=2$ bytes Total page table size $=64 \times 2=128$ bytes Statement C is correct. Physical memory size $=32 \mathrm{~KB}$ Number of frames $=32 \mathrm{~KB} / 1 \mathrm{~KB}=32$ Statement D is correct. Correct options: A, B, C, D

A CPU generates $\mathbf{4 8}-$bit virtual addresses. The page size is $\mathbf{8 ~ K B}$. The processor has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) which can hold a total of $\mathbf{256}$ page table entries and is $\mathbf{2}-$way set associative.

The minimum size of the TLB tag is:

  1. $27$ bits 
     
  2. $28$ bits 
     
  3. $29$ bits 
     
  4. $30$ bits
questions.explanation: TLB Tag Size $=$ Virtual Page Number $(\mathrm{VPN})-$ TLB Index $(S)$ Page Offset $(\mathrm{PO})=13$ bits $$ \mathrm{VPN}=\mathrm{VA} \text { Size }-\mathrm{PO} \text { Size } $$ $\mathrm{VPN}=48$ bits $-13$ bits $=\mathbf{3 5}$ bits $$ \begin{gathered} \text { Number of Sets }=\frac{\text { Total TLB Entries }}{\text { Set Associativity }} \\\\ \text { Number of Sets }=\frac{256}{2}=128 \end{gathered} $$ $\operatorname{TLB} \operatorname{Index}(S)=\log _2($ Number of Sets $)=\log _2(128)=\mathbf{7}$ bits $\operatorname{TLB} \operatorname{Tag Size} =35$ bits $-7$ bits $=\mathbf{2 8}$ bits GO Classes answered Dec 19, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes B JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 10 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. If one page fault is generated every $\mathbf{2} \times \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{6}}$ memory accesses, what is the effective access time for memory? $52 ~\mathrm{ns}$  $90 ~\mathrm{ns}$  $54 ~\mathrm{ns}$  $70 ~\mathrm{ns}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let the page fault service time be $\mathbf{8}$ milliseconds $(\mathbf{m s})$ in a computer with average memory access time being $\mathbf{50}$ nanoseconds $(\mathbf{ns})$. If one page fault is generated every $\mathbf{2} \times \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{6}}$ memory accesses, what is the effective access time for memory?

  1. $52 ~\mathrm{ns}$ 
     
  2. $90 ~\mathrm{ns}$ 
     
  3. $54 ~\mathrm{ns}$ 
     
  4. $70 ~\mathrm{ns}$
questions.explanation: $$ \mathrm{EAT}=(1-p) \times t_m+p \times t_{p f} $$ Where: $\mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{m}}$ (Memory Access Time) $=50 \mathrm{~ns}$ $\mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{pf}}$ (Page Fault Service Time) $=8 \mathrm{~ms}$ $\mathbf{p}$(Page Fault Rate) $=\frac{1}{2 \times 10^6}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{EAT}=\left(1-\frac{1}{2 \times 10^6}\right) \times 50 \mathrm{~ns}+\left(\frac{1}{2 \times 10^6}\right) \times 8,000,000 \mathrm{~ns} \\\\ & \mathrm{EAT}=53.999975 \mathrm{~ns} \end{aligned} $$ Option C is correct

questions.questionText: The following two functions, $\mathrm{F1}$ and $\mathrm{F2}$ , that share a variable $\mathrm{X}$ with an initial value of $5$, execute concurrently. $$ \begin{array}{lccl} \mathrm{F} 1() & & & \mathrm{F} 2() \\ \mathrm{A}=\mathrm{X}+3 ; & & & \mathrm{E}=3 * \mathrm{X} \\ \mathrm{X}=\mathrm{A}-1 ; & & & \mathrm{X}=\mathrm{E}+2 \\ \} & & & \} \end{array} $$ The number of distinct values that $\mathrm{X}$ can possibly take after the execution is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.questionHtml:
The following two functions, $\mathrm{F1}$ and $\mathrm{F2}$ , that share a variable $\mathrm{X}$ with an initial value of $5$, execute concurrently.

$$
\begin{array}{lccl}
\mathrm{F} 1() & & & \mathrm{F} 2() \\
\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{X}+3 ; & & & \mathrm{E}=3 * \mathrm{X} \\
\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{A}-1 ; & & & \mathrm{X}=\mathrm{E}+2 \\
\} & & & \}
\end{array}
$$

The number of distinct values that $\mathrm{X}$ can possibly take after the execution is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.explanation: Case$-1:$ F1 executes before F2 Final value of $X$ will be $23$ Case$-2:$ F2 executes before F1 Final value of $X$ will be $19$ Interleaving execution $\rightarrow$ case $-1:$ F1 overwrites the value written by F2 Final value of $X$ will be $7$ in this case Interleaving execution $\rightarrow$ case $-2:$ F2 overwrites the value written by F1 Final value of $X$ wil be 17 in this case The possible values of $X$ are $\{7,17,19,23\}$ GO Classes answered Dec 19, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 4 JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 10 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. A logical address is divided into a c-bit index to the outer page table , an offset within the page of the inner page table , and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses four bytes . All the pages in the system have the same size. The value of $\mathbf{c}$ is $\_\_\_\_$ (Answer in integer).

Each entry of the inner page table uses four bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

questions.explanation: Page Size $=8192$ bytes Inner Page Table Entry Size $=4$ bytes The number of entries in the inner page table is determined by $2^I$. $$ I=11 \text { bits } $$ Page offset $= 13$ bits $C+1+13=36$ $C+11+13=36$ $\mathrm{C}=12$ GO Classes answered Dec 18, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 2 2 votes Aman Shukla answered Dec 18, 2025 Aman Shukla comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 12 JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 11 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider a system with $4$ processes that share $16$ instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $K$ instances. Resources can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of $K$ that will always avoid deadlock is:
questions.questionHtml: Consider a system with $4$ processes that share $16$ instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $K$ instances. Resources can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of $K$ that will always avoid deadlock is:
questions.explanation: The maximum number of resources that can be held by $N$ processes without causing a deadlock is given by the formula: $$ \text { Max Held Resources }<R $$ $$ \mathbf{4 \times(K-1) + 1 \leq 16} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & K-1 \leq \frac{15}{4} \\\\ & K-1 \leq 3.75 \end{aligned} $$ $$ K \leq 4.75 $$ Since $K$ must be an integer (number of resource instances), the largest integer value of $K$ that satisfies this condition is $\mathbf{4}$. questions.questionText: In a system, there are three types of resources: $\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}$, and $\mathbf{R}$. Four processes, $T_1, T_2, T_3$, and $T_4$ execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation. Consider a state of the system with the Allocation and Max matrices as shown below, and in which the Total System Resources available are $\mathbf{10}$  instances of P, $\mathbf{7}$  instances of Q, and  $\mathbf{8}$  instances of $\mathbf{R}$. \[ \begin{array}{c c c c}  & \text{Allocation} & & \text{Max} \\ & \textbf{P Q R} & & \textbf{P Q R}\\ T_1 & 0\ 1\ 0 & T_1 & 4\ 2\ 2 \\ T_2 & 2\ 0\ 0 & T_2 & 6\ 1\ 3 \\ T_3 & 3\ 0\ 2 & T_3 & 3\ 0\ 3 \\ T_4 & 2\ 1\ 1 & T_4 & 4\ 3\ 2 \end{array} \] From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which of the following is/are true? The system is in a safe state, with a possible safe sequence starting with $T2.$ The system is not in a safe state because $T4$ needs $T2$'s allocated resources to finish. The system is in a safe state The system is not in a safe state, as no process can complete its execution.

\[
\begin{array}{c c c c}
 & \text{Allocation} & & \text{Max} \\
& \textbf{P Q R} & & \textbf{P Q R}\\

T_2 & 2\ 0\ 0 & T_2 & 6\ 1\ 3 \\
T_3 & 3\ 0\ 2 & T_3 & 3\ 0\ 3 \\
T_4 & 2\ 1\ 1 & T_4 & 4\ 3\ 2
\end{array}
\]

  3. The system is in a safe state
     
  4. The system is not in a safe state, as no process can complete its execution.

questions.questionText: Consider the following C code segment: #include <unistd.h> #include <stdio.h> int main() {     int i;     for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) {         pid_t pid = fork();                 if (pid == 0) {             // Child branch             printf("Child %d created in iteration %d\n", getpid(), i);             break; // Exit the loop only for the child process         } else {             // Parent branch             printf("Parent %d created child %d in iteration %d\n", getpid(), pid, i);         }     }         sleep(1);     return 0; } Assuming all $\verb|fork()|$ calls succeed, what is the total number of processes (including the original parent) that will be running immediately before the program terminates?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C code segment:
 

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        pid_t pid = fork();
        
        if (pid == 0) {
            // Child branch
            printf("Child %d created in iteration %d\n", getpid(), i);
            break; // Exit the loop only for the child process
        } else {
            // Parent branch
            printf("Parent %d created child %d in iteration %d\n", getpid(), pid, i);
        }
    }
    
    sleep(1);
    return 0;
}


Assuming all $\verb|fork()|$ calls succeed, what is the total number of processes (including the original parent) that will be running immediately before the program terminates?
questions.explanation: Original Parent (P): Completes both loop iterations. Child 1 (C1): Created during $i=0$, then breaks out of the loop immediately. Child 2 (C2): Created during $i=1$, then breaks out of the loop immediately. The total number of processes running before the program terminates is THREE. questions.questionText: A computer system has $12$ tape drives (reusable resources). There are $n$ processes competing for these resources. Each process may require a maximum of  $5$  tape drives to complete its execution. The maximum value of $n$ for which the system can guarantee to be deadlock-free is:
questions.questionHtml:
A computer system has $12$ tape drives (reusable resources). There are $n$ processes competing for these resources. Each process may require a maximum of $5$ tape drives to complete its execution.

The maximum value of $n$ for which the system can guarantee to be deadlock-free is:
questions.explanation: Let: $R=$ Total number of resources (tape drives) $=12$ $M=$ Maximum number of resources needed by any single process $= 5$ $n=$ Number of processes (what we are solving for) Worst-Case Scenario (Maximum Holding): For $n$ processes, the maximum resources that can be held without any process being able to complete is when all $n$ processes hold $M-1$ resources. $$ \text { Total resources held }=n \times(M-1) $$ Deadlock Condition: To guarantee no deadlock, the total number of resources must be strictly greater than the maximum resources that can be held in a state where no process can finish. $$ R>n \times(M-1) $$ We are looking for the maximum integer $n$ that satisfies this condition. $$ \begin{gathered} 12>n \times(5-1) \\\\ 12>4 n \\\\ n<\frac{12}{4} \\\\ n<3 \end{gathered} $$ Max value of $\mathrm{n}=2$ GO Classes answered Dec 8, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 2 JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 13 JAY_THAKAR

questions.explanation: Explanation: 1. Analyze the Logical AND ( $\verb|&&|$ ) Behavior In C, the expression $\verb|A && B|$ uses short-circuit evaluation. If $\verb|A|$ is False  $(0)$, $\verb|B|$ is not evaluated. $\verb|fork()|$ returns $\verb|0|$ to the child process (False) and a positive PID to the parent process (True). 2. Simulation Trace Let's trace the execution:    1. First $\verb|fork()|$ (F1): Parent (P1): Returns True ( $>0$ ). P1 proceeds to evaluate the second part of $\verb|&&|$. . Child (C1): Returns False ( 0 ). C1 short-circuits . It skips the second $\verb|fork()|$ and the $\verb|if|$ body. C1 prints "GATE".    2. Second $\verb|fork()|$ (F2) (Executed only by P1): Parent (P1): Returns True ( $>0$ ). The condition $\verb|True && True|$ is True. P1 enters the $\verb|if|$ block. Child (C2): Returns False (0). The condition $\verb|True && False|$ is False. C2 skips the $\verb|if|$ body. C2 prints "GATE".    3.

questions.questionText: The following C program is executed on a Unix/Linux system: #include <unistd.h> #include <stdio.h> int main() { int i; int n = 10; // n can be any positive integer for (i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (i % 2 != 0) { fork(); } } return 0; } Determine the total number of processes (including the original parent process) created when the program finishes the loop. $2^n$ $2^{n / 2}$ $2^{\lfloor n / 2\rfloor}$ $2^{[n / 2]}$
questions.questionHtml:
The following C program is executed on a Unix/Linux system:

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
int main()
{
    int i;
    int n = 10; // n can be any positive integer
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (i % 2 != 0) {
            fork();
        }
    }
    return 0;
}


Determine the total number of processes (including the original parent process) created when the program finishes the loop.

  1. $2^n$
     
  2. $2^{n / 2}$
     
  3. $2^{\lfloor n / 2\rfloor}$
     
  4. $2^{[n / 2]}$
questions.explanation: Answer option D The loop runs from i = 0 to 9 because n = 10. Since the condition is (i % 2 != 0) , the fork() call happens only for odd values of i, which are 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9, so it executes 5 times. Every time fork() is called, the number of processes doubles. Therefore, after 5 such calls, the total number of processes becomes 2⁵ = 32, including the original parent process. Hence, the correct answer is 2^(n/2) = 32.

questions.questionText: Consider a distributed file system with $\mathbf{5}$ processes that share $\mathbf{11}$ File Handle (FH) instances. Each process can request a maximum of $\boldsymbol{K}$ instances. Currently, each of the $\mathbf{5}$ processes holds  $\mathbf{2}$  FH instances. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a distributed file system with $\mathbf{5}$ processes that share $\mathbf{11}$ File Handle (FH) instances. Each process can request a maximum of $\boldsymbol{K}$ instances. Currently, each of the $\mathbf{5}$ processes holds $\mathbf{2}$ FH instances.

The smallest integer value of $\boldsymbol{K}$ (the maximum a process can request) such that this current state is always an unsafe state (meaning deadlock is possible) is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: Total Resources $(R): 11$ Total Allocated Resources: $5$ processes $\times ~2$ instances/process $=10$ instances Available Resources (Available): $11-10=\mathbf{1}$ instance Determine the Condition for Unsafe State: A state is always unsafe if the Available resources are insufficient to satisfy the Need of any single process. If no process can complete, the system is deadlocked (unsafe). This requires: $$ \text { Need }>\text { Available } $$ Find the Need in terms of $\boldsymbol{K}$ : The remaining resources a process needs is: $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { Need }=\text { Maximum Request }(K)-\text { Current Allocation (2) } \\\\ & \qquad \text { Need }=K-2 \end{aligned} $$ Substitute the values into the unsafe condition: $$ \begin{gathered} K-2>1 \\\\ K>3 \end{gathered} $$ The smallest integer value that is greater than $3$ is $\mathbf{4}$. questions.questionHtml:
A $\mathbf{2000 ~Kbyte}$ memory is managed using variable partitions but no compaction. It currently has three partitions of sizes $\mathbf{300 ~Kbyte}$, $\mathbf{450 ~Kbyte}$, and $\mathbf{650 ~Kbyte}$ respectively.

Assuming the system uses the Worst Fit allocation strategy, the smallest allocation request (in $\textbf{Kbyte}$) that could be denied is for $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: $~\text{Allocated Space} =300+450+650=1400 ~\text{Kbyte}$ $~\text{Total Free Space} =2000 ~\text{Kbyte} -1400 ~\text{Kbyte} =600 ~\text{Kbyte}$ Determine the Denial Threshold ( $H_{\max }+1$ ): When no compaction is available, a request $R$ is denied due to external fragmentation if $R$ is larger than the size of the largest available contiguous hole ( $H_{\text {max }}$ ), even if the total free space is $\geq R$. The smallest request that could be denied is $H_{\text {max }}+1$. To make this value as small as possible, we must assume a scenario where the largest hole, $H_{\text {max }}$, is also as small as possible. This happens when the total free space is fragmented into many small, approximately equal pieces. Largest Hole $\left(H_{\text {max }}\right)=\frac{\text { Total Free Space }}{\text { Number of Partitions }}=\frac{600 \text { Kbyte }}{3}=200 ~\text{Kbyte}$ The smallest allocation request that could be denied is $\mathbf{H}_{\text {max }}+\mathbf{1}$. Denied Request $=20

questions.questionHtml:
A disk of size $\textbf{1024 M}$ bytes is divided into blocks of $\textbf{32 K}$ bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. In linked allocation, each data block reserves $\textbf{8 bytes}$ to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of $\text{8 bytes}$).

Suppose a file of $\mathbf{4 ~M}$ bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$ and $1 \mathrm{~M}=2^{20}$.

The total number of disk blocks that will be allocated to store this file is $\_\_\_\_$ . Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: The Block Size $(B)$ is $32 ~\text{K}$ bytes, and the Pointer Size $(P)$ is $8$ bytes. Convert 32 K to bytes: $32 \mathrm{~K}=32 \times 2^{10}=32768$ bytes. Usable Data Space ( $D$ ): $$ D=B-P=32768 \text { bytes }-8 \text { bytes }=32760 \text { bytes } $$ The File Size $(F)$ is 4 M bytes. Convert 4 M to bytes: $4 \mathrm{M}=4 \times 2^{20}=4194304$ bytes. The total number of blocks needed ( $N$ ) is the ceiling of (File Size / Usable Data Space): $$ \begin{gathered} N=\left\lceil\frac{F}{D}\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{4194304}{32760}\right\rceil \\\\ N \approx\lceil 128.0156\rceil \\\\ \mathbf{N}=\mathbf{1 2 9} \text { blocks } \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Dec 5, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: A Unix-style i-node has the following pointers: $12$ direct pointers $1$ single indirect pointer $1$ double indirect pointer $1$ triple indirect pointer The disk block size is $2^{14}$ bytes ($16384$ bytes). A disk block address is $64$ bits ($8$ bytes). File offsets and file sizes use $64$-bit integers. What is the maximum possible file size in bytes? $2^{46}$ bytes $2^{47}$ bytes $2^{48}$ bytes $2^{50}$ bytes
questions.questionHtml:
A Unix-style i-node has the following pointers:

  • $12$ direct pointers
  • $1$ single indirect pointer
  • $1$ double indirect pointer
  • $1$ triple indirect pointer

The disk block size is $2^{14}$ bytes ($16384$ bytes).

A disk block address is $64$ bits ($8$ bytes).

File offsets and file sizes use $64$-bit integers.

What is the maximum possible file size in bytes?

 

  1. $2^{46}$ bytes
     
  2. $2^{47}$ bytes
     
  3. $2^{48}$ bytes
     
  4. $2^{50}$ bytes
questions.explanation: Addresses per block $p=\frac{2^{14}}{2^3}=2^{11}$ Direct: $12 \times 2^{14}$ bytes Single indirect: $2^{11} \times 2^{14}=2^{25}$ bytes Double indirect: $\left(2^{11}\right)^2 \times 2^{14}=2^{22} \times 2^{14}=2^{36}$ bytes Triple indirect: $\left(2^{11}\right)^3 \times 2^{14}=2^{33} \times 2^{14}=2^{47}$ bytes Largest term $=2^{47}$ bytes, so maximum possible file size $\approx 2^{47}$ bytes. Answer: B. $2^{47}$ bytes GO Classes answered Dec 1, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: In a system, there are three resource types: $X, Y$, and $Z$. Four processes $P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3$ run concurrently. The Max matrix indicates the maximum demand of each resource type by each process. The Allocation matrix shows the number of instances of each resource currently allocated to each process. \[ \begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc}  & \textbf{Allocation} & & & \textbf{Max} & & \\  & X & Y & Z & X & Y & Z \\ \hline P_0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ P_1 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ P_2 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ P_3 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ \end{array} \] Available resources $=\left(\begin{array}{lll}1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right)$ [1 instance of $\mathrm{X}, 1$ of $\mathrm{Y}, 1$ of Z available] From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true? The system is in a safe state. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $X$ were available. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Y$ were available. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Z$ were available.
questions.questionHtml:
In a system, there are three resource types: $X, Y$, and $Z$.

Four processes $P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3$ run concurrently.

The Max matrix indicates the maximum demand of each resource type by each process.

The Allocation matrix shows the number of instances of each resource currently allocated to each process.

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc}
 & \textbf{Allocation} & & & \textbf{Max} & & \\
 & X & Y & Z & X & Y & Z \\
\hline
P_0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\
P_1 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\
P_2 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\
P_3 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\
\end{array}
\]

Available resources $=\left(\begin{array}{lll}1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right)$ [1 instance of $\mathrm{X}, 1$ of $\mathrm{Y}, 1$ of Z available]

From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true?

  1. The system is in a safe state.
     
  2. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $X$ were available.
     
  3. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Y$ were available.
     
  4. The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Z$ were available.

options.label: A
options.text: The system is in a safe state.

options.label: B
options.text: The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $X$ were available.

options.label: C
options.text: The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Y$ were available.

options.label: D
options.text: The system is not safe, but would be safe if one more instance of $Z$ were available.

questions.explanation: A. Because there is one sequence which we can complete all the processes. questions.questionText: A system has $4$ processes that share $10$ instances of a single resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $M$ instances of the resource. Resources are requested and released one at a time. What is the largest value of $M$ that guarantees the system is deadlock-free?
questions.questionHtml:
A system has $4$ processes that share $10$ instances of a single resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $M$ instances of the resource. Resources are requested and released one at a time.

What is the largest value of $M$ that guarantees the system is deadlock-free?
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{n}=$ number of processes = 4 R = total resource instances = 10 M = maximum demand per process (same for each process) The formula $$ R \geq n \times(k-1)+1 $$ is used to find minimum $\mathbf{\mathrm { R }}$ for given $n$ and $k$ to avoid deadlock, where $k=$ max demand per process. $$ n=4, R=10: $$ $$ \begin{gathered} k \leq 1+\frac{10-1}{4} \\ k \leq 1+\frac{9}{4} \\ k \leq 1+2.25 \\ k \leq 3.25 \end{gathered} $$ So $k_{\text {max integer }}=3$. questions.explanation: “The FCB is already in memory.” The FCB contains: pointer to the first block file size other metadata So the pointer to the first block is already known , no disk read is needed. Write the new block to disk (it is already in memory → just write it). Update its pointer to point to the old first block (done during the write). Update the FCB in memory (no disk access, because FCB is already in memory). Only one write is needed. So, Answer is only 1 disk access. Here, the index block is already in memory , so all shifting happens in RAM , not on disk. You want to insert a new block at the beginning . What needs disk access? Write the new block to disk → 1 write Update the index block in memory only → 0 disk accesses (because index block is already in memory) No other blocks need to be read or written. 3 3 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: We want to remove the block numbered 50 (i.e., the 51st block in the file). In linked allocation, blocks are accessed one after another: Read all earlier blocks — from the 1st block up to the 50th block → 50 reads Then read the 51st block (the one being removed) to obtain the pointer to the next block → 1 read Finally, update the pointer in the 50th block so it directly links to the block after the removed one → 1 write Total disk accesses: 51 reads + 1 write = 52 accesses Correct Answer: 52

  1. Acquiring resources in a predetermined order is one way to avoid deadlock.
     
  2. Rolling back threads is one way to address deadlock once it occurs.

  4. Banker's algorithm is one way to recover from deadlock once it occurs.

questions.explanation: Correct Statements: A and B Explanation: A. Acquiring resources in a predetermined order is one way to avoid deadlock. (TRUE) This is a classic Deadlock Prevention technique. By enforcing a global ordering on locks (e.g., always acquire Lock 1 before Lock 2), you make the "Circular Wait" condition structurally impossible. (Note: While strictly called "Prevention" in OS theory, "avoid" is often used colloquially in multiple-choice questions). B. Rolling back threads is one way to address deadlock once it occurs. (TRUE) This is a Deadlock Recovery technique. Once a deadlock is detected, the OS must break the cycle. It typically does this by preempting resources, killing a process, or rolling a victim process back to a safe checkpoint. C. Deadlock means that no threads are able to make progress. questions.questionText: Consider a system with three threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ and three mutex locks $x, y, z$. Each thread executes the following pseudo-code: $$ \begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l} \textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\ \text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\ \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\ \text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\ \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y) \end{array} $$ All threads execute concurrently. Which of the following sequences of lock acquisitions can lead to a deadlock? $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x})$ $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z})$ $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$ $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with three threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ and three mutex locks $x, y, z$. Each thread executes the following pseudo-code:
$$
\begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l}
\textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\
\text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\
\text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\
\text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\
\text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y)
\end{array}
$$
All threads execute concurrently.

Which of the following sequences of lock acquisitions can lead to a deadlock?

  1. $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x})$
     
  2. $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z})$
     
  3. $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$
     
  4. $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$
questions.explanation: $$ \begin{aligned} & T_{1}: \text { acquires } y \\ & T_{2}: \text { acquires } z \\ & T_{3}: \text { acquires } x \\ & T_{1}: \text { tries to acquire } z \text { (blocked) } \\ & T_{2}: \text { tries to acquire } x \text { (blocked) } \\ & T_{3}: \text { tries to acquire } y \text { (blocked) } \end{aligned} $$ This forms a circular wait: $$ T_{1} \rightarrow y \rightarrow T_{3} \rightarrow x \rightarrow T_{2} \rightarrow z \rightarrow T_{1} $$ Hence, deadlock occurs. questions.questionHtml:
Consider the same system with threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ defined as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l}
\textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\
\text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\
\text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\
\text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\
\text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y)
\end{array}
$$
Initially, the program may experience deadlock due to circular waiting between these threads and $T_{3}$. To fix this, the student modifies $T_{3}$.
Which of the following implementations of $T_{3}$ will make the program deadlock-free regardless of the scheduler?
 

  1. $T_{3} : \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}); \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}); \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{x}); \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$
     
  2. $T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}) ; \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{x}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$
     
  3. $T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(z) ; \operatorname{acquire}(x) ; \operatorname{release}(z) ; \operatorname{release}(x)$
     
  4. $T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}) ; \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{z}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$

questions.questionText: In a system, each lock is a $2$-mutex, meaning up to two threads can hold the same lock simultaneously. A third thread attempting to acquire the same lock will block until one of the two holders releases it. Consider two $2$-mutexes: $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, and three threads: $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$, and $\mathbf{z}$. The following sequence of lock acquisitions occurs: Thread $\mathbf{z}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$. Thread $\mathbf{y}$ acquires $\mathbf{b}$. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{b}$ (blocks). Thread $\mathbf{y}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{a}$ (blocks). At this point, there is a cycle in the wait-for graph (edges from $x \rightarrow y$ and $y \rightarrow x$). Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this situation? The system is in deadlock, since a cycle always implies circular waiting. The system is not in deadlock because $\mathbf{z}$ can release its locks and allow progress. The system will remain blocked indefinitely, even if $\mathbf{z}$ releases its locks. The scheduler must preempt $z$ to ensure progress of $x$ and $y$.
questions.questionHtml:
In a system, each lock is a $2$-mutex, meaning up to two threads can hold the same lock simultaneously.
A third thread attempting to acquire the same lock will block until one of the two holders releases it.
Consider two $2$-mutexes: $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, and three threads: $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$, and $\mathbf{z}$.
The following sequence of lock acquisitions occurs:

  1. Thread $\mathbf{z}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
     
  2. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$.
     
  3. Thread $\mathbf{y}$ acquires $\mathbf{b}$.
     
  4. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{b}$ (blocks).
     
  5. Thread $\mathbf{y}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{a}$ (blocks).

At this point, there is a cycle in the wait-for graph (edges from $x \rightarrow y$ and $y \rightarrow x$).
Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this situation?

  1. The system is in deadlock, since a cycle always implies circular waiting.
     
  2. The system is not in deadlock because $\mathbf{z}$ can release its locks and allow progress.
     
  3. The system will remain blocked indefinitely, even if $\mathbf{z}$ releases its locks.
     
  4. The scheduler must preempt $z$ to ensure progress of $x$ and $y$.

options.label: A
options.text: The system is in deadlock, since a cycle always implies circular waiting.

options.label: B
options.text: The system is not in deadlock because $\mathbf{z}$ can release its locks and allow progress.

options.label: C
options.text: The system will remain blocked indefinitely, even if $\mathbf{z}$ releases its locks.

options.label: D
options.text: The scheduler must preempt $z$ to ensure progress of $x$ and $y$.

questions.explanation: Each lock is a 2-mutex, so two threads can hold the same lock simultaneously. Here, $\mathbf{z}$ holds both $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, while $\mathbf{x}$ shares $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ shares $\mathbf{b}$. When $\mathbf{x}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{a}$, both block - forming a cycle in the wait-for graph. However, this is not a deadlock, because $\mathbf{z}$ can still release both locks. Once $\mathbf{z}$ releases them, $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ can proceed. Hence, the system only experiences $\textbf{temporary waiting}$, not a true deadlock. questions.questionText: Consider a system that manages $\textbf{three resource types:}$ $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$. The total number of available instances of each resource type is given as: $$ A_{\text {total }}=12, \quad B_{\text {total }}=9, \quad C_{\text {total }}=12 $$ Four threads (T1, T2, T3, and T4) have the following current allocations and maximum requirements: $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Thread} & \textbf{Current Allocation (A, B, C)} & \textbf{Maximum (A, B, C)} \\ \hline T1 & (2,1,3) & (4,9,4) \\ \hline T2 & (1,2,3) & (5,3,3) \\ \hline T3 & (5,4,3) & (6,4,3) \\ \hline T4 & (2,1,2) & (4,8,2) \\ \hline \end{array} $$ What can we conclude about the system's current state according to the $\textbf{Banker's Algorithm}$? (There may be multiple correct answers.) The system is in an unsafe state; no safe sequence exists. The system is in a safe state with possible sequence $T 3 \rightarrow T 2 \rightarrow T 4 \rightarrow T 1$. The system will immediately deadlock if $T 1$ makes any additional resource request, even if it does not request its full maximum capacity at once. The system can remain safe if available resources increase to $(3,2,2)$, allowing multiple valid sequences.

questions.explanation: Since the process accesses $N+1$ pages sequentially and memory can hold only $N$ pages, each time a new page is referenced, it will evict the least recently used page  which happens to be the one needed next. Thus, every access results in a page fault and no hits occur. Example sequence: $$ \text { Access } P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} \text { fills memory. } $$ Next access $P_{N+1}$ evicts $P_{1}$. Then accessing $P_{1}$ evicts $P_{2}$, and so on. Hence, every reference causes a fault. $$ \boxed{\text { Hit rate }=0} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 13, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Correct Answer: C. Before granting a new lock to a thread, the system runs a function will_deadlock(lock_to_give) to check whether giving that lock may cause a circular wait (deadlock). \[ \begin{aligned} &\text{function } will\_deadlock(lock\_to\_give): \\[6pt] &\quad start\_lock \leftarrow lock\_to\_give \\ &\quad current\_lock \leftarrow lock\_to\_give \\[10pt] &\quad \left|\begin{aligned} &\text{while }(\text{current_lock is held by some thread}): \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{holder_thread} \leftarrow \text{thread holding current_lock} \\[8pt] &\quad\quad \text{if }(\text{holder_thread is waiting for another lock}): \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{current_lock} \leftarrow \text{lock waited by holder_thread} \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{else}: \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{break // no deadlock further on this path} \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{if }(\text{current_lock} = \text{start_lock}): \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \_\_\_\_\_ [A] \_\_\_\_\_ \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{return True} \\[8pt] &\text{end while} \end{aligned}\right. \\[12pt] &\quad \_\_\_\_\_ [B] \_\_\_\_\_ \\ &\quad \text{return False} \end{aligned} \] Choose the correct combination for [A] and [B]: [A] = "Deadlock found", [B] = "Safe to give the lock" [A] = "Safe to give the lock", [B] = "Deadlock found" [A] = "Deadlock found", [B] = "Deadlock found" [A] = "Safe to give the lock", [B] = "Safe to give the lock"
questions.questionHtml:
In a multithreaded system, threads use locks to control access to shared resources. Before granting a new lock to a thread, the system runs a function will_deadlock(lock_to_give) to check whether giving that lock may cause a circular wait (deadlock).

 

\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{function } will\_deadlock(lock\_to\_give): \\[6pt] &\quad start\_lock \leftarrow lock\_to\_give \\ &\quad current\_lock \leftarrow lock\_to\_give \\[10pt] &\quad \left|\begin{aligned} &\text{while }(\text{current_lock is held by some thread}): \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{holder_thread} \leftarrow \text{thread holding current_lock} \\[8pt] &\quad\quad \text{if }(\text{holder_thread is waiting for another lock}): \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{current_lock} \leftarrow \text{lock waited by holder_thread} \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{else}: \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{break // no deadlock further on this path} \\[6pt] &\quad\quad \text{if }(\text{current_lock} = \text{start_lock}): \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \_\_\_\_\_ [A] \_\_\_\_\_ \\[4pt] &\quad\quad\quad \text{return True} \\[8pt] &\text{end while} \end{aligned}\right. \\[12pt] &\quad \_\_\_\_\_ [B] \_\_\_\_\_ \\ &\quad \text{return False} \end{aligned} \]

Choose the correct combination for [A] and [B]:

  1. [A] = "Deadlock found", [B] = "Safe to give the lock"
     
  2. [A] = "Safe to give the lock", [B] = "Deadlock found"
     
  3. [A] = "Deadlock found", [B] = "Deadlock found"
     
  4. [A] = "Safe to give the lock", [B] = "Safe to give the lock"

options.label: D
options.text: [A] = "Safe to give the lock", [B] = "Safe to give the lock"

questions.explanation: Based on the logic of the deadlock detection algorithm, the correct combination is A . Here is the step-by-step breakdown of the code logic: 1. Understanding the Goal The function will_deadlock(lock_to_give) checks for a circular wait condition. It traces the chain of "who is waiting for whom" to see if granting a new lock will close a loop (create a cycle). Return True : Means "Yes, a deadlock will occur." Return False : Means "No, it is safe; no deadlock." 2. Analyzing Part [A] Inside the while loop, the code follows the chain of dependencies: It looks at who holds the current lock. It sees what lock that holder is waiting for next. It updates current_lock to that next lock. The condition if (current_lock == start_lock) checks if we have arrived back at the lock we started with. Interpretation: We started at start_lock , followed the chain of waiting threads, and ended up back at start_lock . This is the definition of a cycle . Conclusion: A cycle means a deadlock is detected. Code

Assume that our OS uses $\textbf{Banker's Algorithm}$ to allocate resources in order to avoid deadlock. The system contains resources $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$, and there are threads $\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2}$, and $\mathbf{3}$. The

The total amount of resources, the current allocation, and the maximum required by each thread are as follows:


At this point, $\textbf{Thread 1}$ requests all the remaining resources it needs, and Banker's Algorithm must decide whether this request should be granted.
However, the algorithm is $\textbf{buggy}$, whenever it simulates Thread $3$'s completion, it incorrectly assumes that Thread $3$ will fail to release $\mathbf{X}$ units of Resource $\mathbf{C}$ after finishing.
For what value(s) of $\mathbf{X}$ will Thread $1$'s original request not be granted (select all that apply)?

  1. $4$
     
  2. $5$
     
  3. $6$
     
  4. $7$
questions.explanation: 1. Compute currently available resources: $$ \text { Available }=(8,9,10)-(3,3,3)=(5 A, 6 B, 7 C) $$ 2. $T_{1}$ requests all remaining resources: $$ \text { Need }_{1}=(5-1,3-1,3-1)=(4 A, 2 B, 2 C) $$ After granting and completing, $\mathrm{T}_{1}$ releases all of its resources: $$ \text { New Available }=(5,6,7)+(1,1,1)=(6 A, 7 B, 8 C) $$ 3. Next, $T_{3}$ can complete since it needs: $$ \text { Need }_{3}=(7-1,3-1,7-1)=(6 A, 2 B, 6 C) $$ After completion, due to the bug, $\mathrm{T}_{3}$ fails to release $X$ units of Resource C : $$ \text { Available }=(7 A, 8 B, 9-X C) $$ 4. Finally, $T_{2}$ requires: $$ \text { Need }_{2}=(3 A, 8 B, 5 C) $$ For the system to be in a safe state: $$ 9-X \geq 5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad X \leq 4 $$ Therefore, if $X=5,6$, or $7$, the system becomes unsafe and $\mathrm{T}_{1}$ 's request will not be granted. $$ \boxed{X=5,6,7} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 13, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply Saif_VG commented De

questions.explanation: Problem: Select all True statements regarding virtual and physical address spaces. Analysis: A. A process's virtual address space can be larger than the size of the physical address space. TRUE. This is the primary definition and benefit of Virtual Memory. For example, a 32-bit process has a 4GB virtual address space, even if the computer only has 512MB of Physical RAM. The OS handles this via demand paging (swapping pages in/out of the disk). B. The physical address space can be larger than a process's virtual address space. TRUE. Consider a 32-bit application running on a modern 64-bit OS with 32GB of RAM. The process is limited to a 4GB virtual space ($2^{32}$), but the physical RAM (32GB) is much larger. C. A process cannot access more memory than the size of its virtual address space. TRUE. questions.explanation: Video Solution (Must Watch): https://youtu.be/hQL7TbaIPHk?t=19501 The physical address is 11 bits long , and the offset uses 8 bits . Thus, the remaining bits identify the physical frame number : \[ \text{Physical frame bits} = 11 - 8 = 3 \] Hence, there are \(2^3 = 8\) physical frames in total. Each frame can be represented by a 3-bit number (0 to 7). Each L2 page table entry (PTE) stores the frame number, so it requires 3 bits and can take: \[ \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} 2^3 = 8\ \text{possible values (0–7)} \\[4pt] \text{for L2 (Inner) page table entries.} \end{array} } \] Each L1 page table entry points to a second-level page table. Solution of this question: System Setup Virtual address size: \(15\) bits Page size: \(32 = 2^5 \Rightarrow\) offset = 5 bits Two-level paging scheme: \[ \underbrace{5\ \text{bits}}_{\text{outer page table index}} \;\big|\; \underbrace{5\ \text{bits}}_{\text{inner page table index}} \;\big|\; \underbrace{5\ \text{bits}}_{\text{offset}} \] 1️⃣ Translate \( \mathbf{VA = 0x1787} \) \[ 0x1787 = (0001\ 0111\ 1000\ 0111)_2 \] \[ = (001\ 0111\ 1000\ 0111)_2 \quad \text{(ignoring the leftmost 0 since the address is 15-bit)} \] \[ = \underbrace{\boxed{001\ 01}}_{\text{outer index}} \; \underbrace{\boxed{11\ 100}}_{\text{inner index}} \; \underbrace{\boxed{0\ 0111}}_{\text{offset}} \] \[ \text{Outer index} = 00101_2 = 5, \quad \text{Inner index} = 11100_2 = 28, \quad \text{Offset} = 00111_2 = 7. \] Outer lookup: page \(73\)[5] = 0x7F → valid bit = 0 → invalid. \[ \boxed{0x1787 \text{ causes a page fault (invalid outer entry).}}

questions.questionText: Suppose you search for an element $x$ in a sorted array of $N$ elements using a linear search. Each memory page holds $p$ array elements ( $N>p$ ). Assume that the cost of a page fault is much higher than that of a normal memory access. On average, how many page faults will be generated during the linear search? $\frac{N}{2}$ $\frac{N}{2 p}$ $\log \frac{N}{p}$ $\frac{p}{N}$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose you search for an element $x$ in a sorted array of $N$ elements using a linear search.
Each memory page holds $p$ array elements ( $N>p$ ).
Assume that the cost of a page fault is much higher than that of a normal memory access.
On average, how many page faults will be generated during the linear search?
 

  1. $\frac{N}{2}$
     
  2. $\frac{N}{2 p}$
     
  3. $\log \frac{N}{p}$
     
  4. $\frac{p}{N}$
questions.explanation: In a linear search, elements are checked one by one from the start. On average, the desired element is found halfway through the array, so the average number of memory accesses is: $$ \frac{N}{2} $$ The array is divided into pages, each containing $p$ elements. This means: Page 1 contains elements 1 to $p$ Page 2 contains elements $p+1$ to $2 p$ and so on Whenever a new page is accessed for the first time, a page fault occurs. Thus, the number of pages (and hence page faults) accessed on average is: $$ \begin{gathered} \text { Page faults }=\frac{\text { Elements accessed }}{\text { Elements per page }}=\frac{N / 2}{p} \\ \boxed{\text { Average page faults }=\frac{N}{2 p}} \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 12, 2025 • edited Nov 12, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Assume that the cost of a page fault is much higher than that of a normal memory access. On average, how many page faults will be generated during the binary search? $\frac{\log N}{p}$ $\log \frac{N}{p}$ $\frac{N}{2 p}$ $\frac{p}{N}$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose you search for an element $x$ in a sorted array of $N$ elements using a binary search.
Each page holds $p$ array elements ( $N>p$ ).
Assume that the cost of a page fault is much higher than that of a normal memory access.
On average, how many page faults will be generated during the binary search?
 

  1. $\frac{\log N}{p}$
     
  2. $\log \frac{N}{p}$
     
  3. $\frac{N}{2 p}$
     
  4. $\frac{p}{N}$
questions.explanation: In a binary search, the array is repeatedly divided into two halves, and only one half is searched each time. Thus, the number of element accesses required is proportional to $\log N$. On average, the number of memory accesses is: $$ \log N $$ The array is divided into pages, each containing $p$ elements. This means: Page 1 contains elements 1 to $p$ Page 2 contains elements $p+1$ to $2 p$ and so on Since binary search jumps between middle elements of the current search range, these elements are likely to be on different pages. A page fault occurs each time a new page is accessed for the first time. Thus, the number of pages (and hence page faults) accessed on average is: $$ \boxed{\text { Page faults }=\log \frac{N}{p}} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 12, 2025 • edited Nov 12, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider a virtual memory system that uses $\mathbf{2}$-level paging. The page size in this system is $\mathbf{2 5 6}$ bytes. Each individual page table fits exactly into one memory frame, and the size of each page table entry (PTE) is $\mathbf{8}$ bytes. Suppose that there is a process with a virtual address space of size $\mathbf{1 0 2 4 0}\left(\mathbf{1 0 x 2}{ }^{\mathbf{1 0}}\right)$ bytes. Also suppose that the entire address space is in memory. How many valid PTEs will exist in the page tables for this process? $32$ $40$ $42$ $48$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a virtual memory system that uses $\mathbf{2}$-level paging. The page size in this system is $\mathbf{2 5 6}$ bytes. Each individual page table fits exactly into one memory frame, and the size of each page table entry (PTE) is $\mathbf{8}$ bytes.
Suppose that there is a process with a virtual address space of size $\mathbf{1 0 2 4 0}\left(\mathbf{1 0 x 2}{ }^{\mathbf{1 0}}\right)$ bytes. Also suppose that the entire address space is in memory.
How many valid PTEs will exist in the page tables for this process?

  1. $32$
     
  2. $40$
     
  3. $42$
     
  4. $48$
questions.explanation: Each page $=2^{8}=256$ bytes. Number of pages needed $=10240 / 256=40$. These $40$ pages require $40$ PTEs in the second-level page tables. Since each page table can hold $2^{5}=32$ PTEs, we need $2$ second-level tables. Each of these is referenced by one entry in the first-level page table, so there are 2 more PTEs at the first level. Hence, total valid PTEs $=40+2=42$. User-Mode Programs (Preemptible) Bottom Half Interrupt Handlers Top Half Interrupt Handlers Kernel System Service Routines (Preemptible) Choose the correct answer from the options given below: $II \rightarrow I \rightarrow III \rightarrow IV$ $III \rightarrow II \rightarrow I \rightarrow IV$ $III \rightarrow I \rightarrow II \rightarrow IV$ $I \rightarrow IV \rightarrow II \rightarrow III$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following interrupt protection levels in Linux, and arrange them in the increasing order of their priorities.

  1. User-Mode Programs (Preemptible)
  2. Bottom Half Interrupt Handlers
  3. Top Half Interrupt Handlers
  4. Kernel System Service Routines (Preemptible)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $II \rightarrow I \rightarrow III \rightarrow IV$
  2. $III \rightarrow II \rightarrow I \rightarrow IV$
  3. $III \rightarrow I \rightarrow II \rightarrow IV$
  4. $I \rightarrow IV \rightarrow II \rightarrow III$
questions.explanation: The correct order of interrupt protection levels in Linux, from lowest to highest priority, is: User-Mode Programs (Preemptible) : These run at the lowest priority and can be interrupted by almost anything, including the kernel and other user programs. Kernel System Service Routines (Preemptible) : These run in the kernel and have a higher priority than user-mode programs but can still be interrupted by high-priority handlers. Bottom Half Interrupt Handlers : These are part of the interrupt handling process and run in a special context. They have a higher priority than the kernel's main routines but are less time-critical than top half handlers. Top Half Interrupt Handlers : These run with interrupts disabled and have the highest priority. They're designed to execute as quickly as possible to handle immediate hardware events before re-enabling interrupts.

  2. The process could create new subprocesses \& wait for the termination of the subprocesses
  3. The time slice of the process expires and it may join the waiting queue
  4. The process is forcibly removed from the CPU and is put in the Waiting queue due to arrival of an interrupt

questions.explanation: C Chandradev yadav answered Nov 6, 2025 Chandradev yadav comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Ramu Kumar commented Mar 25 reply Follow flag Why this event cannot occur The Ready Queue vs. The Waiting Queue: * The Ready Queue is for processes that have everything they need to run and are just waiting for their turn on the CPU. The Waiting (Blocked) Queue is for processes that cannot run even if the CPU were free because they are waiting for an external event (like a keystroke, a disk read, or a child process to finish). The Timer Interrupt: When a process's time slice (quantum) expires, it hasn't done anything "wrong," and it isn't waiting for I/O. It is still perfectly capable of running. Therefore, the OS moves it directly back to the Ready Queue to wait for its next turn. It never goes to the Waiting Queue for a simple timeout. Analysis of the other options Event Can it occur? Destination I/O Request Yes Waiting Queue (Process must wait for the hardware to finish). C

options.label: A

questions.explanation: Let's evaluate each statement about Privileged Instructions : ✅ (A) “It can only be executed by the Operating System kernel and not by user applications.” ✔ True — only the OS (kernel mode) can execute privileged instructions. ✅ (B) “It is designed to perform operations that can directly affect the hardware or system state such as I/O operations or changing memory management setting.” ✔ True — privileged instructions modify system-critical states (I/O, interrupts, memory maps, etc.). ❌ (C) “User applications can execute privileged instructions if they have the correct permissions.” ✘ False — user mode cannot execute privileged instructions under any permission setting. Attempting to do so causes a trap to the OS. ❌ (D) “It is usually executed in user mode to ensure safety and security.” ✘ False — privileged instructions run in kernel mode , not user mode.

questions.questionText: Read the below passage and answer the questions. The Banker's Algorithm is a critical deadlock avoidance method in operating systems, designed to facilitate resource allocation without causing deadlock. It operates by maintaining information about the maximum resources. Each process may require, the current allocated resources and the available resources in the system. The algorithm checks each resource request to determine, if granting it would leave the system in a safe state, meaning that there is always a sequence in which all processes can complete their execution without getting stuck due to resource unavailability. Each process must specify its maximum demand for each resource type before it starts execution. When a process requests additional resources, the algorithm checks if granting the request will keep the system in a safe state. If so, the resources are allocated otherwise the process must wait until its request can be safely fulfilled. What information is used to determine if a resource request can be granted? Available resources and current allocation of each process CPU utilization of each process Number of processes waiting for resources Arrival time of each process
questions.questionHtml:
Read the below passage and answer the questions.

The Banker's Algorithm is a critical deadlock avoidance method in operating systems, designed to facilitate resource allocation without causing deadlock. It operates by maintaining information about the maximum resources. Each process may require, the current allocated resources and the available resources in the system. The algorithm checks each resource request to determine, if granting it would leave the system in a safe state, meaning that there is always a sequence in which all processes can complete their execution without getting stuck due to resource unavailability. Each process must specify its maximum demand for each resource type before it starts execution. When a process requests additional resources, the algorithm checks if granting the request will keep the system in a safe state. If so, the resources are allocated otherwise the process must wait until its request can be safely fulfilled.

What information is used to determine if a resource request can be granted?

  1. Available resources and current allocation of each process
  2. CPU utilization of each process

questions.questionText: Read the below passage and answer the questions. The Banker's Algorithm is a critical deadlock avoidance method in operating systems, designed to facilitate resource allocation without causing deadlock. It operates by maintaining information about the maximum resources. Each process may require, the current allocated resources and the available resources in the system. The algorithm checks each resource request to determine, if granting it would leave the system in a safe state, meaning that there is always a sequence in which all processes can complete their execution without getting stuck due to resource unavailability. Each process must specify its maximum demand for each resource type before it starts execution. When a process requests additional resources, the algorithm checks if granting the request will keep the system in a safe state. If so, the resources are allocated otherwise the process must wait until its request can be safely fulfilled. What is the primary goal of the Banker's Algorithm? To allocate resources optimally To prevent processes from requesting resources To detect and recover from deadlocks To maximise CPU utilization

questions.questionText: Suppose a processor uses a prioritized round robin scheduling policy. New processes are assigned an initial quantum of length . Whenever a process uses its entire quantum without blocking, its new quantum is set to twice its current quantum. If a process blocks before its quantum expires, its new quantum is reset to . For the purposes of this question, assume that every process requires a finite total amount of CPU time. Scenario (a): Suppose the scheduler gives higher priority to processes with larger quanta. Scenario (b): Suppose the scheduler gives higher priority to processes with smaller quanta. Which of the following is correct regarding the possibility of starvation in the system? Starvation is possible in both scenarios. Starvation is not possible in (a) but possible in (b). Starvation is possible in (a) but not in (b). Starvation is not possible in either scenario.
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose a processor uses a prioritized round robin scheduling policy. New processes are assigned an initial quantum of length . Scenario (a): Suppose the scheduler gives higher priority to processes with larger quanta.
Scenario (b): Suppose the scheduler gives higher priority to processes with smaller quanta.
Which of the following is correct regarding the possibility of starvation in the system?

  1. Starvation is possible in both scenarios.

questions.explanation: Scenario A : Suppose the scheduler gives higher priority to processes with larger quanta. This means that it provides higher priority to the process with larger time quantum (Obvious) But what we can imply from this is that we are assigning higher priority to those process that completes it's entire time quantum and it'll get to return again to execute with double it's time quantum than before and probably getting prioritized again.....So it'll complete it's task eventually and can let everyone execute.... So even if there is some wait time for process with low quantum time we can make sure that there will be no starvation... However Scenario B might cause starvation since those small, I/O-heavy jobs keep coming back with top priority, and a long CPU-heavy job could get stuck waiting forever. Running in parallel means that between any two lines of code in one process, any number of lines of the other process may run. Note that x  is a shared variable which both processes can read/modify, while temp$1$ and temp$2$ are local variables that only the corresponding processes can access. int x = 0; proc1 { int temp1 = x; x = temp1 + 1; temp1 = x; x = temp1 + 1; } proc2 { int temp2 = x; x=temp2 + 1; } Which of the following values are possible for x  after both processes have come to a halt? $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two procedures proc$1$ and proc$2$, which run in parallel after initialising initialising x to $0$. Running in parallel means that between any two lines of code in one process, any number of lines of the other process may run. Note that x is a shared variable which both processes can read/modify, while temp$1$ and temp$2$ are local variables that only the corresponding processes can access.

 

int x = 0;

proc1 {
    int temp1 = x;
    x = temp1 + 1;
    temp1 = x;
    x = temp1 + 1;
}

 

proc2 {
    int temp2 = x;
    x=temp2 + 1;
}

 

Which of the following values are possible for x after both processes have come to a halt?

  1. $0$
  2. $1$
  3. $2$
  4. $3$
questions.explanation: The possible flow of execution leads us to three possible values 1,2,3. So options B,C,D are correct and A is not Correct. For value 1:  Say t2=x happens first and then it gets preempted and process 1 executes completely ,  and then x = t2+1 happens that is 1, so all the updates by process 1 are lost.  For value 2 :  Similar to above , all updates by process two are lost. Or we can make the execution in such a way that atleast one increment operation gets lost. For value 3 :  All values increments gets used.

questions.questionText: C12. Consider the following information about a magnetic hard disk, with cylinders numbered 0 (innermost) to 511 (outermost): at time \(t = 0\) ms, the disk head is at cylinder 120, moving outwards towards cylinder 511; the disk arm takes \(1\) ms to seek from cylinder \(i\) to cylinder \(i + 1\) or cylinder \(i − 1\); the time taken to read sectors may be neglected. The following \(I/O\) requests arrive at the disk controller. Request no. Arrival time (ms) Cylinder no. \(r_1\) 1 480 \(r_2\) 10 240 \(r_3\) 15 360 \(r_4\) 20 100 \(r_5\) 25 140 \(r_6\) 30 185 (a) In what order will the six requests be serviced if the controller uses the following scheduling algorithms?         i. look         ii. preemptive SHORTEST SEEK TIME FIRST (SSTF) The standard definitions of these algorithms are given towards the end of this question. (b) Let \(T_{LOOK}\) (S) and \(T_{SSTF} (S)\) denote the total time taken to service a given sequence \(S\) of requests using look and SSTF , respectively. Two requests arrive at time \(t = 0\)  for cylinder nos. \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Show that, for any \(x_1\), \(x_2  \in [0, 511]\)  , \( T_{LOOK} (S) \geq  T_{SSTF} (S) \ for \  S = x_1, x_2 \). In LOOK , the disk head alternatively moves in the outward and inward directions servicing any currently pending requests as it reaches each cylinder.  While travelling in a particular direction, the arm goes only as far as the last request currently pending in \( that \ direction\) , before reversing direction. In preemptive SHORTEST SEEK TIME FIRST (SSTF) , the disc controller runs the scheduling algorithm whenever a new I/O request arrives.
questions.questionHtml:
C12. Consider the following information about a magnetic hard disk, with cylinders numbered 0 (innermost) to 511 (outermost):

  • at time \(t = 0\) ms, the disk head is at cylinder 120, moving outwards towards cylinder 511;
  • the disk arm takes \(1\) ms to seek from cylinder \(i\) to cylinder \(i + 1\) or cylinder \(i − 1\);
  • the time taken to read sectors may be neglected.

The following \(I/O\) requests arrive at the disk controller.

Request no.Arrival time (ms)Cylinder no.
\(r_1\)1480
\(r_2\)10240
\(r_3\)15360
\(r_4\)20100
\(r_5\)25140
\(r_6\)30185

(a) In what order will the six requests be serviced if the controller uses the following scheduling algorithms?
        i. look
        ii. preemptive SHORTEST SEEK TIME FIRST (SSTF)
The standard definitions of these algorithms are given towards the end of this question.
 

(b) Let \(T_{LOOK}\) (S) and \(T_{SSTF} (S)\) denote the total time taken to service a given sequence \(S\) of requests using look and SSTF , respectively. Two requests arrive at time \(t = 0\)  for cylinder nos. \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Show that, for any \(x_1\), \(x_2  \in [0, 511]\)  ,
\( T_{LOOK} (S) \geq  T_{SSTF} (S) \ for \  S = x_1, x_2 \).

In LOOK, the disk head alternatively moves in the outward and inward directions servicing any currently pending requests as it reaches each cylinder. 

While travelling in a particular direction, the arm goes only as far as the last request currently pending in \( that \ direction\) , before reversing direction.
In preemptive SHORTEST SEEK TIME FIRST (SSTF) , the disc controller runs the scheduling algorithm whenever a new I/O request arrives.

B) cat "$@" 

C) Both a and b

questions.explanation: The correct answer is: ✅ (B) cat "$@" Explanation: (A) cat $.  ❌ Incorrect This is not a valid shell variable. This command will either give an error or treat $. as a literal filename, which is incorrect. (B) cat "$@" ✅ Correct "$@" expands to all command-line arguments individually, preserving spaces. This ensures that cat reads and displays each argument (file) one by one, even if filenames contain spaces. (C) Both A and B ❌ Incorrect (D) cat "$." ❌ Incorrect This is not a valid shell variable, so the command is incorrect.

questions.questionText: A computer system supports a logical address space of $2^{32}$ bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of $4096$ bytes. A logical address is divided into a $b$-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size. The value of $b$ is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.questionHtml:
A computer system supports a logical address space of $2^{32}$ bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of $4096$ bytes. A logical address is divided into a $b$-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of $b$ is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Logical Address Space $= 2^{32}$ Bytes Page Size $= 4096$ Bytes $= 2^{12}$ Bytes Page Table Entry Size $($at inner page table$)$ $= 8$ Bytes $= 2^{3}$ Bytes It is given that there is two-level hierarchical paging, with $b-$bit index to the outer page table. Now, as given all pages in the system have the same size. So, $1$ Page Table should fit in $1$ Page. Therefore, Page Table Size $=$ Page Size. Page Table Size $= 2^{12}$ Bytes Page Table Size $=$ No. of Entries $\times$ Page Table Entry Size So,  No. of Entries $\times$ Page Table Entry Size $= 2^{12}$ Bytes No. of Entries at inner level$= \frac{2^{12}}{2^{3}} = 2^{9} $ As, no. of entries are $2^{9}$ at inner level, $9$ bits would be required for index at that level. So, $x=9$ $b+x+12 = 32$ $b=32-12-9$ $b=11$ Answer : Value of $\mathbf{b}$ is $\mathbf{11}$    benzene06 answered Feb 28, 2025 • edited Feb 28, 2025 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Share Follow See all 15 Comments 15 15 Comments reply Show 12 pre

questions.excerpt: A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive...
questions.questionText: A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows: $M_{1}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{1}>P_{3}>P_{2}>P_{4}$, i.e., $P_{1}$ and $P_{4}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively. $M_{2}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{2}>P_{3}>P_{4}>P_{1}$, i.e., $P_{2}$ and $P_{1}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively. A process $P_{i}$ is scheduled to a processor $M_{k}$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_{j}$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds? $9.00$ $8.75$ $6.50$ $7.50$
questions.questionHtml:
A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

  • $M_{1}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{1}>P_{3}>P_{2}>P_{4}$, i.e., $P_{1}$ and $P_{4}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
  • $M_{2}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{2}>P_{3}>P_{4}>P_{1}$, i.e., $P_{2}$ and $P_{1}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process $P_{i}$ is scheduled to a processor $M_{k}$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_{j}$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?

  1. $9.00$
  2. $8.75$
  3. $6.50$
  4. $7.50$
questions.explanation: Processes and Burst Times: P₁ → 20 ms P₂ → 16 ms P₃ → 25 ms P₄ → 10 ms All arrive at time 0 . Processor M₁ Priority: P₁ > P₃ > P₂ > P₄ (P₁ has highest, P₄ has lowest) Processor M₂ Priority: P₂ > P₃ > P₄ > P₁ (P₂ has highest, P₁ has lowest) Scheduling Simulation: We simulate time step-by-step using non-preemptive scheduling and whichever processor is free . Time 0: Both processors free M₁ will prefer P₁ (highest priority) M₂ will prefer P₂ (highest priority)  Assign: M₁ → P₁ (20 ms) M₂ → P₂ (16 ms) Time 16: M₂ becomes free Only P₃ and P₄ remain. Based on M₂ priority: P₃ > P₄ → Assign P₃ (25 ms)  Assign: M₂ → P₃ from time 16 to 41 Time 20: M₁ becomes free Only P₄ remains → Assign to M₁ (10 ms)  Assign: M₁ → P₄ from time 20 to 30 Process Start Time Burst Time Completion Time Waiting Time = Start - Arrival P₁ 0 20 20 0 P₂ 0 16 16 0 P₃ 16 25 41 16 P₄ 20 10 30 20 Average Waiting Time: 0+0+16+20/4=9 Sunnychxfyhc answered Apr 11, 2025 Sunnychxfyhc comment S
